lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'metal has a thin, invisible layer of dirt on its surface'. The layer is tarnish (oxide) formed by air, not dirt, and dirt is something flux does not mainly remove. Flow 4: the soldering iron is first defined inside the safety paragraph ('the hot tool used for this work'), and then paragraph 3 introduces it again from the start ('A soldering iron heats a replaceable metal tip.'). Paragraph 3 also ends with a side detail about solder paste and reflow ('These parts are often joined with a solder paste that melts when the whole board is heated.'), and the chain does not need it before flux and wetting. Clarity 4: that same reflow sentence adds a second process (heating a whole board) that a beginner does not need here. The flashcards cover solder paste and reflow.

Also 'Each track can let you hear its incoming sound always, never, or only while it is set to record.' -> 'On each track, you choose to hear the incoming sound always, never, or only while the track is set to record.' Re-run check-lesson.mjs and confirm the result is 480 words or fewer.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'The first samplers were large, costly machines' is loose, because the earliest tape-replay instruments in the term list (Chamberlin, Mellotron) were not digital samplers. 'Large instruments keep only the start of each sound in memory...' and 'Finished instruments are sold as libraries' are absolutes; many libraries are free and not every large instrument streams from disk. Scope 4: slicing and time-stretching (Beat Slicing, REX File, slice marker, slicing mode, transient slicing, Time Stretching and others, about 6-7%) are not mentioned. The tape-replay group (Mellotron, tape attack, tape strip and others) is reduced to one sentence. Flow 4: paragraph 6 jumps from drum layering to history ('The first samplers were...'), then to hardware and software. That is the one break in an otherwise clean chain. Clarity 4: 'where the wave crosses the center line' assumes the reader has seen a waveform drawing. Language 4: 'makers' first appears without saying makers of what, and 'a physical box' is informal.
lessons.comment: Strong lesson. It moves clearly from one recording to a playable instrument: root key, loops, multisampling, velocity layers, round robin, drums, formats and clearance. All six named terms match their glossary plain English. The check script passes (478 words). The fixes below drop the history and streaming sentences, which removes the inaccurate absolutes and the flow jump. That frees room for a slicing sentence so the lesson stays under 480 words. Weighted score 4.2 (B).
lessons.fixes: 1) Accuracy plus flow: delete 'The first samplers were large, costly machines.' and change 'Today, all of this runs inside an instrument, either a physical box or a program in recording software.' -> 'All of this runs inside an instrument, either a hardware unit or a program in recording software.' (this also fixes 'physical box'). 2) Accuracy plus length: delete 'Large instruments keep only the start of each sound in memory and read the rest from the drive.' (streaming stays in the flashcards). Also 'Finished instruments are sold as libraries' -> 'Finished instruments are often sold as libraries'. 3) Scope: after 'A drum hit usually plays once, to its end.' add 'A recorded drum loop can also be cut at each hit, so each hit plays from its own key.' 4) Language: 'So makers record many notes, each with its own group of keys.' -> 'So the makers of sampled instruments record many notes, each with its own group of keys.' 5) Clarity: 'Its ends are usually placed where the wave crosses the center line' -> 'Its ends are usually placed where the drawn wave of the sound crosses its center line'. Re-run check-lesson.mjs and confirm the result is 400-480 words.

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the topic has 296 terms. Station imaging (sweepers, jingles, liners, sonic logos, imaging voice, promos) is a large group and gets one short sentence. News production (newscast, voicer, actuality, wrap, rip and read, rundown, sound on tape, wire service) gets half a sentence. The remote and commentary group and the programming group are covered well. Flow 3: paragraph 3 ends on the sweeper, which has nothing to do with the playout sentence before it. Paragraph 4 reads as a tour of rooms. Paragraph 6 jumps to television and concert control rooms ('in the same way') without a reason. Paragraph 7 lists four separate things (delay, silence, compliance recording, emergency alerts) and marks the list with 'Last,', which is the kind of side list the standard bans. Clarity 4: 'mixing board', 'channel' and 'the whole mix' are used without a plain description, and a beginner may not know them. Language 4: there is personification in 'The station also protects itself from silence' and 'the law ... asks stations'. Accuracy 5: every claim checks out against the glossary (clockwheel, traffic log, mix-minus, IFB, dump button, master control room, silence detector, compliance recording), and the A1/A2 simplification is acceptable. Glossary 5: board operator, hitting the post, clockwheel, sweeper, mix-minus, traffic log, dump button and master control room all exist in the topic and agree with their plain English. The two script warnings ('board operator' and 'hitting the post') match 'Board Op / Board Operator' and 'Hit the Post'. Opening/closing 5: an everyday studio scene leads into the organizing question, and the closing names the ratings group in plain words. House rules 5: the script passes with 0 fails (480 words, 8 paragraphs). It is at both upper limits, so any fix must not add net words.
lessons.comment: Accurate, and the glossary agreement is clean. The programming chain (clockwheel, traffic log, playout) and the mix-minus/IFB explanation are good. The main weakness is flow: the second half turns into a list of rooms, then TV and concert control rooms, then a four-item 'Last,' paragraph. Imaging and news production are underrepresented for a topic whose Welcome text puts imaging up front. Weighted 4.3 (B). The lesson is at 480 words and 8 paragraphs, so the fixes below delete about as many words as they add.
lessons.fixes: FLOW (para 3 to 4, also SCOPE imaging). Delete 'A short clip that says the station's name over music is called a sweeper.' from the end of para 3. Replace 'Sweepers and advertisements are usually recorded in production rooms.' with 'Short clips that say the station's name over music are called sweepers. They and the advertisements are usually recorded earlier in production rooms, so every hour sounds like the same station.' SCOPE (news). Replace 'News is often read from a small booth, between short recorded reports.' with 'News is often read live from a small booth, with short recorded reports from reporters between the stories.' FLOW (para 6). Delete 'Television and concert broadcasts use their own control rooms in the same way.' This saves the words for the additions above. FLOW and LANGUAGE (para 7). Replace 'The station also protects itself from silence. Machines can detect silence on the output and start backup audio. Last, the law in many countries asks stations to prove what they broadcast, so they often record everything that goes on air.' with 'Silence on the air is another danger, so a silence detector watches the output and starts backup audio. Because the law in many countries requires stations to prove what they broadcast, they often record everything that goes on air.' ('Silence detector' is in the term list.) CLARITY. Replace 'So the board sends each caller the whole mix except their own voice.' with 'So the board sends each caller all the program sound except their own voice.' Replace 'each connect to their own channel on a mixing board' with 'each connect to their own volume control, called a channel, on a mixing board'. If this goes over 480 words, shorten 'Imagine sitting beside the host of a live morning show at a radio station.' to 'Imagine sitting beside the host of a live morning radio show.' Re-run check-lesson.mjs after the fixes.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Loudness rules apply on every route' is an absolute that is not true. Commercial loudness laws mainly cover television, and in many countries radio has no legal loudness rule. 'Stations keep loudness records as proof' generalizes in the same way. 'A quiet tone tells a stereo radio to separate the two' suggests an audible tone, but the stereo pilot is also too high to hear. Scope 4: all large groups are present: contribution/STL links, processing, modulation and FM multiplex/RDS, digital radio and TV sound systems, loudness and compliance. Transmitter monitoring and remote control get one tacked-on sentence. Streaming appears only in the closing, and compliance reports get a few words. Flow 4: the chain order is good, but 'Emergency alerts are often sent as tones inside the sound.' is tacked onto the end of the FM multiplex paragraph. 'Engineers can also watch and control the transmitter from far away.' is tacked onto the end of the loudness paragraph, where it does not belong. Clarity 4: 'peak' is used before it is described. Paragraph 5 packs stereo sum, difference subcarrier, pilot, RDS and emergency alerts into one paragraph, which is dense for a beginner. Language 4: 'route' in 'on every route' is vague, and 'the sound changes a radio wave' and 'AM radio changes the strength' make the radio the actor in a loose way. Glossary 5: air chain, overmodulation, dialogue normalization, studio-transmitter link, on-air processor and radio data system all exist in the topic and agree with their plain English. Opening/closing 5: the listener-in-a-village scene is different from sibling 4090's in-studio scene and leads to the question, and the closing is clean. House rules 5: the script passes with 0 fails (480 words, 8 paragraphs; the FM and 'listening' warnings are fine). It is at both upper limits, so fixes must not add net words.
lessons.comment: A clear, well-ordered walk down the air chain from contribution links to transmitter, processing, multiplex, digital and TV, and loudness. The glossary agreement is clean. One absolute ('Loudness rules apply on every route') needs to be softened, and two sentences are left hanging at paragraph ends (emergency alerts, transmitter remote control). Weighted 4.2 (B). The lesson is at the 480-word cap, so the fixes are word-neutral or shorter.
lessons.fixes: ACCURACY. Replace 'Loudness rules apply on every route, so an advertisement should not be much louder than the program around it.' with 'In many countries, loudness rules apply to television, so an advertisement should not be much louder than the program around it.' ACCURACY. Replace 'Stations keep loudness records as proof.' with 'Television stations often keep loudness records as proof.' ACCURACY. Replace 'A quiet tone tells a stereo radio to separate the two.' with 'A low tone, also too high to hear, tells a stereo radio to separate the two.' FLOW and SCOPE (monitoring). Delete 'Engineers can also watch and control the transmitter from far away.' from para 7. Then, in para 2, after 'Then the studio-transmitter link carries it to the transmitter, often far away, by radio or over the internet.', add 'Engineers usually watch and control that transmitter from the studio.' FLOW. Replace 'Emergency alerts are often sent as tones inside the sound.' with 'Emergency alerts can also travel in this signal, as special tones in the sound.' CLARITY. Replace 'If a peak goes past the limit,' with 'If the loudest moments, the peaks, go past the limit,'. LANGUAGE. Replace 'At the transmitter, the sound changes a radio wave. AM radio changes the strength of the wave, and FM radio changes its frequency.' with 'At the transmitter, the sound is used to change a radio wave. In AM radio it changes the strength of the wave, and in FM radio it changes its frequency.' SCOPE (streaming) and word budget. Replace 'Television can also carry a second soundtrack, such as another language.' with 'Television can carry a second soundtrack, such as another language, and online streams carry the same processed sound.' To pay for the added words, replace 'Between the studio and the transmitter, the sound passes through many pieces of equipment.' with 'On its way to the transmitter, the sound passes through much equipment.' and delete 'often' in 'often in separate frequency bands'. Re-run check-lesson.mjs and confirm 480 words or fewer.

lessons.reasons: Flow 4: paragraph 4 has only two sentences and stands apart. It could sit after the jobs paragraph or after the coverage paragraph and nothing would be lost, and paragraph 6 is almost as short. Clarity 4: the sentence about how the work is bought ('installers offer prices on finished plans') squeezes the design-build and design-bid-build ideas into one clause that a beginner cannot follow. It also sits inside the needs-analysis paragraph, where it does not belong. Glossary 4: the name 'priority paging' is given after two sentences, and the second one ('heard where a local volume control is turned down') describes Priority Page Override. In the glossary, Priority Paging only means the page lowers or cuts the music.
lessons.comment: A strong, accurate lesson. It follows the life of an installed system from questions, site survey, jobs, zones, coverage and rooms, through documents, installation and commissioning, to service, and every large group is there. The check script passes (476 words, 8 paragraphs). Three small fixes would bring it to a 5: tie the short zone paragraph into the chain, make the sentence about how the work is bought clearer, and name priority paging before the volume-override sentence. Weighted score 4.6 (A).
lessons.fixes: Glossary: 'An important announcement usually lowers or cuts the music. It is also heard where a local volume control is turned down. This is called priority paging.' -> 'An important announcement usually lowers or cuts the music. This is called priority paging. The announcement is often heard even where a local volume control is turned down.' | Clarity: 'The owner also chooses whether one company designs and builds the system, or installers offer prices on finished plans.' -> 'The owner also chooses how the work is bought. A central digital processor decides what plays in each area and sends each source to the right zones.' -> join it to the end of paragraph 3: 'These jobs are often different in different areas. Each area with its own sound and its own volume is called a zone. A central digital processor decides what plays in each zone.' This removes the stand-alone paragraph and leaves 7 paragraphs.

Clarity 4: 'A host may guide guests on the stage' and 'tiny lights' (for OLED) give the reader no clear picture. Language 4: 'tiny lights' is vague, and 'A host may guide guests on the stage' can be read in more than one way.
lessons.comment: It covers the whole topic well: distributed and constant-voltage wiring, taps, displays and connections, echo cancelling, automixing, and assisted listening, and the four named terms match the glossary. The check script passes (475 words, 7 paragraphs). The main weakness is the event paragraph, which breaks the single meeting thread and says little. Weighted score 4.1 (B).
lessons.fixes: Flow/Scope/Clarity: replace paragraph 3 ('In the meeting room, the speakers make the voice clear rather than loud. At a larger event, several people give talks, and their microphones, music and slides follow a planned order. A host may guide guests on the stage. The team practices this order in advance. Some events are also streamed to people watching online.') with: 'The same room is sometimes used for a larger event, such as a company meeting with several speakers. lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the group of sounds a car makes on purpose (engine sound enhancement, active sound management, pedestrian alert sounds) and phone connection in the car are not mentioned. lessons.comment: A clear, accurate lesson. It follows the system from the head unit, through power and grounding (with the fuse safety point early), the amplifier, speakers and enclosures, cabin acoustics and the vehicle's own noise, to boats, aircraft and emergency vehicles. lessons.fixes: Flow: move 'Heavy mats on the doors and floor reduce panel vibration.' from paragraph 5 into paragraph 6, after 'They then reduce the loudest paths first.', and write it as: 'Heavy mats on the doors and floor reduce the vibration of the panels.' | Scope: replace 'Some cars use their speakers to cancel road noise.' with 'Some cars use their speakers to cancel road noise, and some also add sounds on purpose, such as engine sound inside the cabin or a warning sound outside for people walking near a quiet electric car.' (In the flashcards these are active sound management and the pedestrian alerting system; this sentence leaves them unnamed.)

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Other venues have no roof over the audience' is stated as a fact for every amphitheater, but many open-air venues (sheds) have a roof over the front seats; the glossary says 'usually'. Scope 4: venue types, house, mix positions, backstage, loading and safety are all there, but the worship group (about 24 of 143 terms, ~17%: chancel, sanctuary, narthex, choir loft, organ loft, transept, cry room, fellowship hall...) gets one short paragraph, and the seating-section names (balcony, dress circle, loge, box seating, aisles, accessible seating) get only a brief mention. lessons.comment: Clear, accurate tour of a venue from the lobby to the loading dock, with a good everyday opening and a matching close. The real blocker is the word count (493). After that, soften the amphitheater absolute and tie the church paragraph more firmly into the chain. Weighted about 4.2 (B), but it cannot be approved until the script passes.
lessons.fixes: HOUSE RULES (493 words, need 400-480): delete 'So designers check the sound and view from these seats carefully.' (11 words) and 'In some buildings, a freight elevator then takes cases to the stage.' (12 words). That brings it to about 470. CLARITY: 'In a black-box theater, a plain dark room, the stage and seats can be moved for each show.' -> 'A black-box theater is one plain dark room. Its stage and seats can be set up differently for each show.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Whatever holds the load, the maker's table, called a load chart, shows how much it may hold' extends the load chart to every holding system. The glossary defines a load chart as the maker's table for a truss (by span and by spread or point load); other hardware is rated by its working load limit. Glossary 4: the load chart is used more widely than its glossary meaning (see Accuracy). House rules 3: the check script fails the lesson at 482 words (limit 480).
lessons.comment: Strong safety-first chain: the dangers come early, and the counterweight, trim, motor and ground support paragraphs each grow from the one before. Two things block approval: the lesson is 2 words over the limit, and the last body paragraph reads as a parts list with an over-wide load-chart claim. lessons.fixes: HOUSE RULES (482 words, need 400-480): delete 'A sudden jolt can go past it.' (repeats the next sentence) and change 'In many theaters, long metal pipes hang' -> 'Long metal pipes hang'. That brings it to about 473. A frame holds less at one spot than when weight is spread along it.' -> 'For a frame of metal tubes, the maker's table, called a load chart, shows how much it may hold. lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'The closing door shakes back and forth' reads as the door's swinging motion. The sound actually comes from the quick vibration when the door hits its frame. Scope 4: live list is 211 terms (matches the snapshot). Period (One-Cycle Time, Frequency-Period Relationship) and superposition/interference (Superposition, Wave Superposition, Constructive/Destructive Interference) are big groups, and both are in the Welcome. The lesson describes them but never names them. Wave shapes (plane, spherical, wavefront, transverse) are not mentioned, which is acceptable for a small group. Flow 4: the last paragraph jumps from phase to materials with no bridge, then packs in speed, impedance and resonance. 'The sound of the door does not repeat.' is a side remark. Clarity 4: the decibel paragraph packs in the reference, decibels, the logarithmic step, sound power and intensity. 'Each equal step up on this scale multiplies the pressure by the same number' is abstract for a beginner. Language 4: 'Audio compares each sound's pressure' gives the subject a human action (personification). 'an even, regular shape' is vague. Glossary 4: sound intensity is given as 'the energy passing through each area' and leaves out 'each second', which the glossary has. All other named terms (compression and rarefaction, longitudinal wave, frequency, wavelength, sine wave, amplitude, phase, resonant frequency) match their plain English.
lessons.comment: A strong, accurate physics chain that opens from an everyday scene and keeps the air-motion idea correct. The check script passes (478 words, 8 paragraphs, avg 11.7, 1 sentence over 20). Main polish: name period and superposition, cut the abstract log-step sentence, and bridge into the materials paragraph. Weighted 58/14 = 4.1 (B). The fixes below net about +1 word (about 479), so re-run the script after applying them.
lessons.fixes: ACCURACY: 'The closing door shakes back and forth.' -> 'When the door hits its frame, it shakes back and forth very quickly.' | FLOW (word budget): delete 'The sound of the door does not repeat.' | SCOPE: after 'The length of one cycle is called the wavelength.' add 'The time of one cycle is called the period.' | SCOPE: 'When two waves reach the same place, their pressures add together.' -> 'When two waves reach the same place, their pressures add together. This is called superposition.' | CLARITY: delete 'Each equal step up on this scale multiplies the pressure by the same number.' | FLOW: 'Sound travels faster in stiffer materials.' -> 'The material also matters: sound travels faster in stiffer materials.' | LANGUAGE: 'Audio compares each sound's pressure with a fixed reference' -> 'In audio, each sound's pressure is compared with a fixed reference' | LANGUAGE: 'an even, regular shape' -> 'a simple, regular shape' | GLOSSARY: 'the energy passing through each area, drops with distance' -> 'the energy passing through each area each second, drops with distance' | BUDGET: 'The flashcards explain each of these ideas in detail, including the math behind them.' -> 'The flashcards explain each of these ideas in detail.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Only qualified people open power equipment that is switched on' is incomplete as safety advice. Work on live equipment also needs written permission and protective clothing, and the lesson never mentions the arc danger. 'A house usually receives one alternating wave' is softened with 'usually', so it is acceptable. Scope 4: live list is 286 terms (matches the snapshot). The arc-flash group (Electrical Arc, Arc Flash Awareness/Boundary/PPE Category/Risk Assessment, Incident energy, Approach Boundaries, Energized Electrical Work Permit) is missing. The isolation transformer from the Welcome is missing. Power supplies (SMPS, linear, rectifier, inverter, hold-up time) get only one clause. Flow 4: the chain is sound, but paragraph 5 carries too much. Clarity 3: paragraph 5 has about 11 sentences and 8 concepts (single phase, three phase, feeder, distro, breaker, voltage drop, power factor, load sizing). A beginner will feel this overload, and the power-factor sentences are the hardest part. Language 4: 'makes the case live' uses trade jargon that a second-language reader may take literally. Glossary 4: 'ground-fault device' is not in this topic's term list, and it mixes 'ground' with the 'protective earth' wording just before it. Voltage, current, power distro, voltage drop, power factor, AC/DC, single/three phase and circuit breaker all agree with the glossary.
lessons.comment: A good safety-first chain. The dangers and the never-break rules come early, as the standard requires, the opening is everyday, and the closing is clean. The check script passes (479 words, 7 paragraphs, avg 13.7, 4 sentences over 20). The main weakness is the overloaded distribution paragraph; split it. Also complete the live-work safety rule and add the arc danger. Weighted 56/14 = 4.0 (B), with clarity at 3 to fix before approval. The fixes below net about 480 words, so re-run the script and trim one more short phrase if needed.
lessons.fixes: CLARITY (3): split paragraph 5 into two paragraphs before 'Every cable also loses some voltage along its length.' The result is 8 paragraphs, with no word change. | ACCURACY: 'Only qualified people open power equipment that is switched on.' -> 'Only qualified people, with permission and protective clothing, work on power equipment that is switched on.' | SCOPE: after '...so you cannot let go.' add 'A short circuit can also cause a burning flash called an electrical arc.' | LANGUAGE: 'If a fault makes the case live' -> 'If a fault connects the case to a powered wire' | GLOSSARY: 'In many places, a ground-fault device also switches off the power when a small current leaks away.' -> 'A second safety switch can also turn off the power when a small current leaks to earth.' | FLOW/BUDGET: 'With these rules in place, a crew can plan the supply.' -> 'Then the crew plans the supply.' | BUDGET: 'A concert stage needs the same on a much larger scale.' -> 'A concert stage needs far more.' | BUDGET: 'The flashcards explain shock, grounding and the safety rules, and how power is supplied, distributed and protected.' -> 'The flashcards explain each of these ideas in detail.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'A thin, hollow sound can mean one cable has its two signal wires swapped' leaves out the condition that makes it true. One reversed cable on its own sounds normal. A hollow sound comes only when that signal mixes with another copy of the same sound and partly cancels (the glossary 'Hollow sound' says this). Flow 4: paragraph 6 is a run of noise types listed one after another (hum, howl, hollow, digital, network, wireless), and paragraph 4 on test tools is a short side step. Clarity 3: paragraph 6 packs ground current, feedback, polarity, clock sync, computer overload, packet loss, firmware and RF into one paragraph, which is too much for a beginner on a first read. Language 4: the phrasal verb 'drop out'. House rules 2: the check script FAILS at 508 words (limit 400-480). Scope 5: the method (symptom, half-split, substitution, tracing, isolation), test tools, common and intermittent faults, noise diagnosis (ground, feedback, polarity, digital, network, RF), thermal faults and root cause all appear in proportion. Glossary 5: all six named terms exist in the topic and agree with their plain English (checked live; 241 terms match the snapshot).
lessons.comment: A clear method lesson with a strong concert opening. The mute-first and do-not-open-equipment safety points come early, and the term coverage is very good. It cannot pass until it is under 480 words. The same edit that shortens it should also break up the crowded noise-diagnosis paragraph. One accuracy fix is needed on the swapped-wire hollow-sound claim. Weighted 4.0 (B), and it is blocked by the script failure. Aim for 460-470 words after the fixes.
lessons.fixes: 1) House rules / clarity / flow (paragraph 6), saves about 20 words: 'In digital equipment, clicks and gaps can mean the devices do not share one timing signal, or the computer cannot process the sound fast enough. On an audio network, gaps can also come from lost data or mismatched device software.' -> 'In digital equipment and on audio networks, clicks and gaps often mean a timing problem, lost data, or a computer that cannot keep up with the sound.' 2) Language / house rules, saves about 4 words: 'Wireless microphones can drop out from a weak battery, a damaged antenna, or strong radio signals nearby.' -> 'Wireless microphones can lose their signal because of a weak battery, a damaged antenna, or strong radio signals nearby.' (If more words must go, use 'Wireless microphones can lose their signal from a weak battery or strong radio signals nearby.') 3) Accuracy (adds about 9 words): 'A thin, hollow sound can mean one cable has its two signal wires swapped.' -> 'A thin, hollow sound can mean one cable has its two signal wires swapped, so its sound partly cancels another copy of the same sound.' 4) House rules, saves about 7 words: 'The method starts with what you notice. The sign of a problem that you notice is called the fault symptom.' -> 'The method starts with the sign of a problem that you notice, which is called the fault symptom.' 5) House rules, saves about 5 words: 'Good sound there means the fault comes later. Bad sound there means it comes earlier. You divide the half with the fault into two again and again.' -> 'If the sound is good there, the fault comes later; if not, it comes earlier. You keep dividing the faulty half in two.' 6) Closing, saves 3 words and drops a new idea: 'and the names of common faults, including crew slang.' -> 'and the names of common faults.' 7) If still over 470, delete 'One person changes things at random; another follows a calm method.' (11 words); the question that follows still states the method. Re-run check-lesson.mjs and confirm 0 fails.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: two mixing practices are stated too absolutely: 'Engineers also give each part its own frequency range.' and 'So the main part is usually the loudest.' Both are common starting points, not rules. Flow 4: the chain moves from levels to timing to microphone timing to placement to balance to hearing, but five paragraph openers rely on 'also' ('must also control timing', 'Timing also matters', 'also places', 'must also be balanced', 'can also lead'). So it reads as a list of separate checks more than one argument. Clarity 4: 'Clicks also appear when two devices both set the timing.' is too short for a beginner to understand a clock-master conflict. Language 4: 'Level between the two speakers also places each sound.' is an unusual structure that is hard to read literally. Scope 5: gain staging and overload, latency and clocking, phase and polarity, stereo placement and mono, masking and hierarchy, and perception, references and translation are all present. Glossary 5: audio latency, polarity mismatch, mono compatibility, level masking and reference track all exist and agree (checked live; 84 terms). House rules 5: 475 words, 8 paragraphs, 0 fails.
lessons.comment: A strong lesson that covers a broad mixed topic. The phone-playback opening sets the question (equipment, settings, mix or hearing) and the closing answers it. The remaining polish: soften two mixing absolutes, make the clocking sentence clear, and replace a few 'also' links with real transitions. Weighted 4.4 (B). Keep the word count at 480 or below when adding words (it is at 475 now). The fixes below add about 14 words, so trim the same number elsewhere: for example, cut 'They also play the mix on small speakers and in a car.' (12 words), because 'Translation' is left to the flashcards.
lessons.fixes: 1) Accuracy: 'So the main part is usually the loudest. Engineers also give each part its own frequency range.' -> 'So the main part is often the loudest. Engineers often give each part its own main frequency range.' 2) Clarity: 'Clicks also appear when two devices both set the timing.' -> 'Clicks can also appear when two connected devices both try to control the timing, instead of one leading.' 3) Language: 'Level between the two speakers also places each sound.' -> 'The level of a sound in each of the two speakers decides where you hear it.' 4) Flow: 'A digital system must also control timing.' -> 'Even with good levels, a digital system can fail on timing.' and 'The parts must also be balanced against each other.' -> 'Once each part has its place, the parts must be balanced against each other.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the tinning group (Tinning, Pre-Tinning, Tip Tinner, Tinned Wire, Brass Sponge: tip and wire preparation) gets no mention, although it is a core part of everyday bench soldering. The other groups are covered: safety, iron and tips, flux and wetting, joint inspection and defects, and desoldering and rework. Lead versus lead-free solder is covered briefly. Accuracy 5: the burns, fire, fume and asthma, and lead-hygiene claims are correct and agree with the glossary. 'Solder Fume' says burnt flux can permanently cause asthma. The tip, flux, fillet, cold-joint, disturbed-joint, bridge, lifted-pad and hot-air claims are all true. Glossary 5: solder, flux, wetting, fillet, desoldering and cold solder joint all match their plain English (checked live; 88 terms).
lessons.comment: An excellent lesson. It opens on a concrete object (the inside of a guitar plug), puts safety early in the chain, and builds a clean line: heat, then flux, then wetting, then the fillet shape, then defects, then desoldering and repair. It reads clearly and literally. The only gap is tip and wire tinning. Weighted 4.9 (A).
lessons.fixes: Scope: in paragraph 3, after 'The iron heats a replaceable metal tip.', add: 'The tip is kept coated with a thin layer of fresh solder so heat passes into the joint well. Coating a tip or a wire end with solder before the joint is made is called tinning.' (about 35 words; the lesson goes to about 495, so cut about 20 words elsewhere, for example shorten 'Tiny surface parts are often removed with a hot air tool that melts all their joints at once.' to 'Tiny surface parts are often removed with hot air.' and delete 'A fine tip suits the tiny parts that sit on the surface of many circuit boards.'). Re-run check-lesson.mjs.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'This fading time' refers to a time the text never set up, and the SBIR sentence says it is 'the same kind of canceling' as room modes, but modes are standing waves and SBIR is interference between direct and reflected sound. Scope 4: all large groups are present (reflections/decay, clarity, modes, absorption, diffusion, isolation, HVAC noise, boundary interference), but the concert-hall measures (strength, intimacy, liveness, bass ratio, stage support, ITDG) appear only as 'clarity', and resonance/damping (Q, underdamped) is missing. Flow 4: paragraph 5 starts on low notes with no bridge from clarity, and its last sentence (speaker near a wall) is added on at the end. Clarity 4: 'Above the Schroeder frequency' uses a term before saying what it is, and paragraph 5 packs modes, the Schroeder frequency and SBIR together. Language 4: 'lively' is a vague sound adjective that is never explained.
lessons.comment: A clear, well-ordered lesson with an everyday opening and a correct closing. Every named term matches the glossary, and the check script passes (476 words, 8 paragraphs, 0 fails; its only warning is 'Schroeder', which is a term from the list). The weak spots are paragraphs 3 and 5: an unclear 'fading time', and a dense modes paragraph with an added SBIR sentence. Weighted score is about 4.2 (B). The lesson is at 476 words, so any additions need cuts, for example 'The room made the difference.'
lessons.fixes: ACCURACY/CLARITY: 'This fading time is the most common measure of a room.' -> 'The time the sound takes to fade away is the most common measure of a room.' | ACCURACY/FLOW: 'The same kind of canceling happens near a wall, where a speaker's reflection can weaken some bass.' -> 'A related problem happens near a wall: the sound reflected from the wall can cancel some of the speaker's direct bass.' | FLOW: 'Low notes have long waves, sometimes as long as the room.' -> 'Low notes behave differently, because their waves are long, sometimes as long as the room.' | CLARITY: 'Above the Schroeder frequency, so many modes overlap that the level becomes more even.' -> 'At higher frequencies, so many modes overlap that the level becomes more even. The frequency where this change happens is called the Schroeder frequency.' | LANGUAGE: 'It keeps the room lively without strong single echoes.' -> 'It keeps sound reflecting around the room without strong single echoes.' | SCOPE: after 'Speech usually needs more of it than music.' add 'Concert halls are also described by how loud and how close the sound seems to listeners.' To make room, cut 'The room made the difference.' and 'The bass is then too loud in some places and too quiet in others.' can become 'The bass then changes from place to place.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'cannot be corrected this way' is an absolute; ordinary minimum-phase EQ cannot correct excess phase, but FIR correction can sometimes reduce it. Scope 4: measurement, magnitude/phase/group delay, impulse response and the mathematics are all present, but the large transform and time-frequency group (Fourier, FFT, STFT, wavelets, cepstrum, Hilbert, about 45 terms) gets only two compressed sentences. Flow 4: the sentence about the fast version and 'related methods' reads as an aside inside the impulse-response paragraph. Clarity 3: 8 named terms (the standard is 2-6), and paragraph 3 (magnitude, phase response, the rate of phase change, group delay) and paragraph 7 (complex number, convolution, linear and time-invariant assumptions, z-domain filters and stability) are too dense for a 16-year-old on first read. Language 4: 'cut the sound into short moments' and 'Behind every step so far' are not literal. Glossary 4: the minimum-phase description does not use the glossary's key idea, 'adds the least delay possible'. Opening/closing 4: 'what its two parts mean' is unclear (magnitude and phase, or the two views?), and the closing leaves out the mathematics from what the learner will know. House rules 4: 8 named terms is over the standard's 2-6, the lesson sits at exactly 480 words, and 'zero to one' adds numbers.
lessons.comment: An accurate and well-ordered introduction to a hard topic: comparison, then the two parts, then reliability, then the time view, then correction, then the mathematics. The opening is everyday and does not repeat the Welcome text. The script passes (480 words, 8 paragraphs, 0 fails; its only warning is 'Fourier', which is a term from the list). The main weakness is density: too many named terms, and two paragraphs that pack several abstract ideas together. Weighted score is about 3.9 (C). Fix the clarity items before approval. Any additions need equal cuts, because the lesson is at the 480-word cap.
lessons.fixes: CLARITY/HOUSE (cut to 7 or fewer named terms): 'How much the system raises or lowers each frequency is called the magnitude.' -> 'How much the system raises or lowers each frequency is its level.' (magnitude stays in the flashcards). | CLARITY: 'When every frequency is delayed by the same time, the phase changes at a steady rate as frequency rises. How fast the phase changes shows how late each frequency arrives. This is called group delay.' -> 'Phase and time are linked. The faster the phase changes from one frequency to the next, the later those frequencies arrive. This delay is called group delay.' | CLARITY: 'Digital filters are designed with the same mathematics, written in a special form that also shows whether a filter stays stable.' -> 'Digital filters are designed with the same mathematics.' | ACCURACY: 'Extra delay that the levels do not predict, often from a reflection, cannot be corrected this way.' -> 'Extra delay that the levels do not predict, often from a reflection, usually cannot be corrected by an ordinary equalizer.' | GLOSSARY: 'Such a system is called a minimum-phase system, and an equalizer can usually correct it.' -> 'Such a system adds the least delay possible for its levels. It is called a minimum-phase system, and an equalizer can usually correct it.' | FLOW/SCOPE/LANGUAGE: 'Computers use a fast version, and related methods cut the sound into short moments to show how frequencies change.' -> 'Computers use a fast version. Related methods study a sound in short parts, one after another, to show how its frequencies change over time.' | LANGUAGE: 'Behind every step so far is one kind of mathematics.' -> 'Every step so far uses the same kind of mathematics.' | OPENING/CLOSING: 'what its two parts mean, and when the data can be trusted.' -> 'what its level and timing parts mean, when the data can be trusted, and which mathematics links them.' | HOUSE: 'So the analyzer scores each frequency from zero to one.' -> 'So the analyzer gives each frequency a reliability score.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: says every electrolytic has a plus and a minus end, but the topic's own list has bipolar electrolytic and non-polar capacitors. Scope 4: resistor types (carbon-film, metal-film, wirewound, thick and thin film, about 25 terms, a large group) are left out, even though the opening asks 'what makes one type better than another'. The parts named for their job (bypass, coupling, decoupling, cathode, emitter, pull-up resistors, about 35 terms) get only one sentence. Varistor and Zener protection are missing. Flow 4: the sentence about parts named for their job sits in the middle of the capacitor paragraph and covers resistors too. Paragraph 7 ('Other passive parts…') is a catch-all side block. Clarity 4: 'from one stage to the next' uses 'stage' before the reader knows what a stage is. Language 4: 'it decides how the part behaves' gives the layer a human action (personification).
lessons.comment: A clear, accurate chain of parts (resistor, capacitor, dielectric, inductor, diode) that matches the glossary. It passes the script at exactly 480 words, so any added text needs an equal cut. Main weaknesses: one absolute statement about polarity, resistor types left out, and a catch-all last paragraph. Weighted 4.2 (B).
lessons.fixes: 1) Accuracy: 'It has a plus end and a minus end, and one connected backwards can burst.' -> 'Most have a plus end and a minus end, and one connected backwards can burst.' 2) Scope: after 'The real value can differ from it by a small allowed amount.' add 'Resistors are made from carbon, metal film or wound wire, and each kind adds a different amount of noise.' To keep 480 words or fewer, cut 'Some special metals are used as covers that reduce magnetic hum.' 3) Flow and clarity: move 'Many capacitors and resistors are named for the job they do in a circuit. One may pass a signal from one stage to the next, and another may keep a supply voltage steady.' to the end of paragraph 4. Change 'from one stage to the next' to 'from one part of a circuit to the next'. 4) Language: 'The insulating layer is called the dielectric, and it decides how the part behaves.' -> 'The insulating layer is called the dielectric. Its material sets much of how the part behaves.' 5) Flow: open paragraph 7 with a link from the diode paragraph instead of 'Other passive parts respond to the world around them.' For example: 'Some parts change their resistance on purpose, with heat or light.' Then keep the thermistor, light and crystal sentences.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: two small absolutes. 'They become very hot' is not always true, since it depends on class and load. 'The most important active component is the transistor' is an opinion stated as fact. Current mirror and cascode stages, and transistor noise and limits (burst, flicker, Early effect, secondary breakdown), are left out. lessons.comment: A strong single chain: weak signal, transistor, stages, output and safe operating area, chips, digital circuits, microcontroller. Every named term agrees with the glossary. It is at 478 words, so any addition needs a cut. Weighted 4.5 (A).
lessons.fixes: 1) Accuracy: 'They become very hot.' -> 'They often become very hot.' 'The most important active component is the transistor.' -> 'The basic active component is the transistor.' 2) Scope: after 'That amount is the gain.' add 'Different types of operational amplifier are made for low noise, low distortion, or a wide output range.' To make room, cut 'for example one that reads the buttons and shows the menus' (end the sentence at 'It runs a small program.'). 3) Clarity: 'In one main type, a small current at the control connection does this. In the other type, a voltage does it, and almost no current flows into that connection.' -> 'There are two main types. In one, a small current at the control connection does this. In the other, a voltage does it, and almost no current flows in.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: faders and slide potentiometers (a key term group) are not mentioned, because the lesson speaks only of knobs. Displays (LED, LCD, VFD, Nixie, seven-segment) and the mechanical reverberators the Welcome names (spring, plate, tape echo) are missing. Power parts (rectifier, choke, battery hazards) get one aside each. Flow 3: paragraph 7 is a catch-all with no link to paragraph 6. It joins attenuator pads, meters, frame hardware, backplanes and heat sinks in one paragraph. 'All of these parts are held in place by hardware' could be moved anywhere. The battery sentence in paragraph 6 is also an aside. Clarity 4: paragraph 7 brings in about five new ideas at once. Opening/closing 4: 'Imagine sitting at a mixing console… Inside, small parts move' is close to the 'Imagine opening a guitar amplifier. Inside…' opening of sibling 3780 in the same batch.
lessons.comment: Paragraphs 2–5 (potentiometer and taper, switch and encoder, relay, transformer and turns ratio) are an accurate, well-linked chain that agrees with the glossary. The lesson weakens in paragraphs 6–7, which turn into a list of leftover parts. It is at 477 words, so adding to it means cutting. Weighted 4.4 (B).
lessons.fixes: 1) Flow (score 3): split paragraph 7 and link each part to the chain. Replace paragraph 7 with: 'Once the signal has passed through these parts, its level often needs to be lowered or shown. A few resistors can lower the level by one fixed amount. This group is called an attenuator pad. A needle meter or a row of small lights shows how high the level is.' Then move the hardware sentences to the end of paragraph 6, where the subject is power and heat: 'Power parts get hot, so metal plates called heat sinks carry heat away. In larger equipment, circuit boards often slide into a frame and plug into a shared board at the back.' Delete 'All of these parts are held in place by hardware.' 2) Flow: cut 'Portable equipment often gets its power from a battery instead of the wall socket.' or join it to the fuse sentence ('Equipment that runs on a battery needs the same protection.'). 3) Scope: in paragraph 2, after 'This part is called a potentiometer.', add 'The same part also comes as a slider, called a fader, which moves in a straight line.' (fader is in the term list). Pay for it by cutting 'Each one does one job'-type repeats elsewhere, or the battery sentence. 4) Opening: change the scene so it differs from 3780's look inside an amplifier. For example: 'Imagine turning the volume knob on a radio, pressing a power button, and watching a level light flash. Each of these acts moves or touches a small part.' lessons.reasons: Scope 4: quality systems and process control (6 Sigma, statistical process control, process capability, acceptable quality level, the quality-management system) are reduced to 'a sample from each batch'. Revision and traceability (engineering change order, revision number, date code, lot code) and enclosure finishing (anodizing, powder coating, potting) are missing, though each group is small. lessons.comment: An accurate, well-ordered chain from breadboard to PCB, design files, packages, reflow assembly, inspection, yield and compliance. The opening is unique in the batch and every named term matches the glossary. It is at 479 words, so any addition needs an equal cut. Weighted 4.6 (A).
lessons.fixes: 1) Flow and clarity: move 'Designers often prefer parts that a second company also makes, in case one part stops being made.' to the end of paragraph 5 (packages), changed to: 'Designers often prefer a part that a second company also makes in the same case, in case one maker stops.' 2) Scope: in paragraph 7, after 'The percentage of boards that pass is called yield.' add 'Factories track this number over time, and each change to the design gets a new revision number.' To stay at 480 words or fewer, cut 'the metal that is melted to join parts' to 'the melted metal that joins parts', and cut 'and each copy is slightly different' from paragraph 2.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: it says 'Older recognizers use several parts' and then sets that against 'Newer recognizers often use one large program, called a neural network'. This suggests older systems had no neural networks, but hybrid HMM-DNN acoustic models (in the term list) are neural networks. It also calls a neural network 'one large program', when a neural network is a kind of model, not the whole system. Scope 4: speech recognition, text-to-speech, speaker recognition, anti-spoofing and datasets are all in the chain. Speech enhancement (Krisp, RNNoise, Auphonic, Enhance Speech, Cleanvoice, echo cancellation model) gets only half a sentence. The speech-quality metrics group (DNSMOS, NISQA, ViSQOL, MCD, non-intrusive speech quality assessment) is not mentioned anywhere, not even in the closing. Flow 4: paragraph 4 says error counting is needed because intent recognition needs correct words, which is a weak link. Paragraph 6 opens with 'A related program', but the previous paragraph was about text-to-speech, so 'related' points to nothing. Clarity 4: paragraph 6 packs diarization, embeddings, enrollment, verification, two error types, the threshold trade-off and spoofing into one paragraph. Glossary 4: 'neural network' is named ('called a neural network'), but it is not a term in this topic's list. It could pass as a plain parent word of 'Neural language model' or 'Time-delay neural network', but the definition given is loose.
lessons.comment: Strong, accurate overall (B). The opening scene carries the whole topic, there are no brands, the check script passes with 0 fails and the snapshot holds 166 terms, matching live. Fix the neural-network framing and give speech enhancement and quality measurement a place. Keep the total at 480 words or fewer; it is 478 now, so any addition needs a matching cut.
lessons.fixes: Accuracy/Glossary: change 'Newer recognizers often use one large program, called a neural network, that learns from examples to go directly from sound to text.' to 'Newer recognizers often use one large learned model that goes directly from sound to text.' This removes the unlisted named term and the false contrast. Flow: change 'A related program marks which person spoke at each moment in a recording with several voices.' to 'Recognizing the voice itself, not only the words, is the next job. One program marks which person spoke at each moment in a recording with several voices.' Flow: change 'That only works if the words are correct, so engineers count the mistakes.' to 'Every later step depends on correct words, so engineers count the mistakes.' Scope: change 'Other programs first remove noise and echo, so the speech is easier to recognize.' to 'Other programs first remove noise and echo, so the speech is easier to recognize and to listen to.' Then change the closing to 'The flashcards cover each step, from detecting and cleaning speech and writing it as text to computer voices, speaker checks, ways to measure speech quality and the shared recordings used to test them.' To save words, cut 'especially during silence' to 'often during silence', and cut 'It reads an answer aloud, and it may even check that the voice is really yours.' to 'It reads an answer aloud and may check that the voice is yours.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'small processors built only for sound math' is too absolute; DSP chips are built for signal math in general, not only sound. 'They briefly raise the sample rate' reads as 'for a short time', but oversampling raises the rate inside the effect for as long as it runs. 'Some store numbers only within a limited range' is vague, since every number format has some limit; what matters is that fixed-point formats have a narrow range. Scope 4: music information retrieval is about a fifth of the 238 terms (recommendation, classification, transcription, fingerprinting, similarity), but it gets one short paragraph that names only onset, beat, tempo, chords and key. Deepfake detection and the rights and law terms are missing from the ethics paragraph. The emerging group (cloud and browser studios, digital twin, TinyML, federated learning) appears nowhere, not even in the closing. Flow 3: paragraph 3 is a list of three unconnected techniques (number range, long reverbs, oversampling). Paragraph 4, 'A filter is a calculation…', does not grow from paragraph 3. Paragraph 6, 'A computer voice can copy a real person', jumps from song identification to voice cloning with no link. Clarity 3: paragraph 3 assumes knowledge a beginner lacks. 'Sample rate' is never explained, and 'held at the limit' and 'unwanted tones' are abstract. A 16-year-old would not follow why a value 'turns into loud noise'. Language 4: 'sound math' is informal, 'briefly' is ambiguous, and 'the sound part of the program' is vague. Opening 4: the sentence 'Some audio software changes sound, some studies music, and some can copy a person's voice.' jumps from the singing scene straight to voice copying.
lessons.comment: Accurate and glossary-faithful, with all six named terms matching their plain English. Grade C (3.9): the topic is three separate areas, and the chain does not yet join them. The adaptive-filter paragraph and the voice-cloning paragraph each start fresh, and paragraph 3 is a list. The check script passes with 0 fails, and the snapshot holds 238 terms, matching live. The lesson is 479 words, so every addition below comes with a cut.
lessons.fixes: Clarity/Flow para 3: replace 'To meet the deadline, digital mixing consoles often use small processors built only for sound math. Some store numbers only within a limited range. A value past that range is usually held at the limit, because otherwise it turns into loud noise. Engineers use faster ways to run long echoes and reverbs. They briefly raise the sample rate when an effect could create unwanted tones.' with 'To meet the deadline, digital mixing consoles often use small chips built for fast signal math. Many of these chips can store only a narrow range of numbers. A value that grows too large is usually held at the highest value, because otherwise it jumps to a wrong value and makes loud noise. Programmers also use faster methods for long reverbs, and some effects work at a higher sample rate inside, which is more sound values each second, to avoid unwanted tones.' Flow para 4 opening: change 'A filter is a calculation that makes some frequencies louder or quieter.' to 'Many of these calculations are filters, which make some frequencies louder or quieter.' Flow para 6 opening: change 'A computer voice can copy a real person.' to 'Software that can recognize a song can also be used to copy a real person's voice. Checking whether a voice or a file is real is the last question.' Then add 'Other software checks whether a voice is computer-made.' after 'audio watermarking'. Scope para 5: after 'It names the chords and the key.' add 'It can also sort music by style and suggest songs a listener may like.' Scope closing: change 'The flashcards cover audio code and chips, efficient processing, music analysis, and the rules for training data and computer-made voices.' to 'The flashcards cover audio code and chips, efficient processing, music analysis, new ways of working online, and the rules for training data and computer-made voices.' Opening: change 'Some audio software changes sound, some studies music, and some can copy a person's voice.' to 'Other software studies music, and some can even copy a voice.' To stay at 480 words or fewer, cut 'So the sound part of the program should not wait for slower work, such as loading a file.' to 'So the audio code should not wait for slower work, such as loading a file.', cut 'at a steady rate' from paragraph 2, and cut 'and keeps correcting itself' to 'and corrects itself'.

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: localization and the precedence effect are about a fifth of the 157 terms (cone of confusion, localization blur/dominance, precedence buildup/breakdown, echo threshold, Clifton/Franssen effects, minimum audible angle, ventriloquism, better-ear listening, spatial release from masking), but they get only four short sentences, and the precedence effect is missing entirely. Recruitment also arrives in the two-ears paragraph as a second idea. Clarity 4: 8 dense paragraphs. Paragraph 6 packs three annoyance causes, rating scales, effort, fatigue and distraction together. Its idea 'a judgment, not a meter reading' repeats the Welcome's 'Loudness is a perception, not a meter reading' twice, in P1 and in the closing (rule 22).
lessons.comment: I checked it against the live data: 157 terms, which matches the snapshot, and the six named terms match their plain_english (binaural summation agrees with the glossary's 'about one and a half times, not double'). The script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns. All claims are accurate and hedged ('often', 'usually', 'can'). The everyday opening is strong. Main weaknesses: the localization/precedence group is thin, there is one jump into paragraph 6, the lesson is dense, and the Welcome's key phrase is echoed. Weighted 61/14 = 4.4 (B).
lessons.fixes: Scope 4: 'Two ears also tell us where a sound is. A sound in front and the same sound behind can be easy to confuse.' -> 'Two ears also tell us where a sound is. When a sound and its echo arrive close together, we usually hear one sound, placed where the first sound came from. A sound in front and the same sound behind can still be easy to confuse.' Then cut a sentence elsewhere to stay under 480 words (for example, delete 'Unwanted speech can also take attention away from a task.'). || Flow 4: 'Listeners can rate how loud a sound seems, or which level feels most comfortable. Yet level is only one part of comfort.' -> 'All of this changes how comfortable a place is to listen in. Listeners can rate which level feels most comfortable, yet level is only one part of comfort.' || Clarity 4: 'Speech in noise or strong echoes takes extra mental work to understand. That work is called listening effort. After many hours of it, the ears and brain become tired. That work is called listening effort, and after many hours of it, the ears and brain become tired.' || Language 4: 'Hearing damage can also change how each ear builds loudness.' -> 'Hearing damage can also change how loud sounds seem to each ear.' || House rules 4: 'By the end, you will know why loudness is a judgment and not a meter reading, and what makes a place easy or difficult to listen in.' -> 'By the end, you will know how the ears and brain judge loudness and place sounds, and what makes a place easy or difficult to listen in.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Every sound mixes low, middle and high frequencies' is an absolute that is false (a pure tone has one frequency). Whole-sound and character words (clean, natural, clinical, vintage, lo-fi, musical, transparency) get half a sentence. Flow 4: the end of paragraph 6 ('Some words are not about a region at all. Gritty... snappy...') is a side block that belongs with paragraph 2's 'Others describe the whole sound'. Clarity 4: seven named terms (the standard is 2-6), and 'distortion' is used without a plain explanation. Language 4: 'feels rough and tiring' uses the vague sound adjective 'rough', and 'where many instruments have sound' is vague. lessons.comment: I checked it against the live data: 220 terms, which matches the snapshot. All named terms exist, and muddy, warm, boxy, nasal, harsh, midrange and coloration match their plain_english except the small muddy range point. The script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns. The region-by-region chain is clear and well ordered, and the requests and ear-training groups are present. The weakest part is the frame: the opening scene and the closing idea repeat the Welcome text, and the closing makes an unverified claim about flashcard order. Fix the one absolute, the region-less side block and the high-region coverage. Weighted 55/14 = 3.9 (C).
lessons.fixes: Accuracy 4: 'Every sound mixes low, middle and high frequencies, and engineers divide them into named regions.' -> 'Most sounds mix low, middle and high frequencies, and engineers divide them into named regions.' || Scope 4: 'Many tone words describe the high frequencies. When the highest frequencies are missing, the sound seems dull and far away.' -> 'Many tone words describe the high frequencies. The very highest part is often called air. When it is missing, the sound seems dull and far away.' (Air is in the term list; this adds one named term, so the separate side block below must be removed to stay at six or fewer.) || Flow 4: delete 'Some words are not about a region at all. Gritty describes added distortion, and snappy describes how sharply a drum hit starts.' from paragraph 6. Change paragraph 2's 'Others describe the whole sound, such as clean or natural, or the balance from low to high.' -> 'Others describe the whole sound, such as clean or natural, the balance from low to high, or how sharply a drum hit starts.' || Clarity 4: 'That is called boxy.' -> 'People call this a boxy sound.' (this keeps the description but drops a named term, bringing named terms to six or fewer). || Language 4: 'When the upper midrange, just below the high frequencies, is too loud, the sound feels rough and tiring. That is called harsh.' -> 'When the upper midrange, just below the high frequencies, is too loud, the sound is tiring to hear. That is called harsh.' AND 'Just above is the lower midrange, where many instruments have sound.' -> 'Just above is the lower midrange, where many instruments have the body of their sound.' || Glossary 4: 'With too much there, instruments become hard to tell apart. By the end, you will know what engineers usually mean by each tone word, which frequency region it describes, and how a request is linked to a change in sound.' || House rules 4: covered by the boxy and gritty/snappy edits above (named terms down to six or fewer, and word count lower).

lessons.reasons: Scope 3: the 234-term list has a large silent-film and early cinema music group, about 25 terms or 10% or more (photoplay music, photoplay album and library, Kinothek, compiled accompaniment, compilation score, stock cue, hurry, misterioso, agitato, furioso, melodrama, overture, entr'acte, curtain and exit music, incidental music), and the lesson leaves it out entirely. The playing-technique and texture group (divisi, con sordino, spiccato, tutti, soli, octave doubling, extended technique, aleatoric writing, tone cluster, sound mass) gets no more than a hint, because paragraph 7 talks about instruments only in terms of dialogue. Flow 3: paragraphs 6 and 7 are joined by add-on links ('Harmony matters as well', 'The choice of instruments matters too'). You could move or drop either one without breaking the chain. Paragraph 7 also changes subject halfway, from the dialogue pocket to orchestration and score preparation. lessons.comment: Accurate and well grounded: the opening is strong, and the spotting, cue and hit-point chain is clear. Two things weaken it: it leaves out the silent-film and stock-music side of the topic, and the harmony and orchestration paragraphs read like a list of extra aspects rather than the next link in the chain. Overall: weighted 4.1, grade B. Minor point on the title: 'Film Scoring Composition and Orchestration' drops the separator from 'Film Scoring - Composition & Orchestration', so 'Film Scoring Composition' reads as one phrase. Check this against the batch's title convention.

(19 words) and 'Each player then gets a separate part.' (7 words). lessons.comment: A clean, accurate chain: time, then mouth shape, then body and voice, then the conflict with meaning, then delivery. The language is plain throughout. It needs three things: a better balance between translation choices and deliverables, a clear referent for isochrony, and a link into the delivery paragraph. Overall: weighted 4.6, grade A.
lessons.fixes: CLARITY: Change 'The new line should start when the mouth opens and stop when it closes. This rule of equal length is called isochrony.' to 'The new line should last as long as the original line, starting when the mouth opens and stopping when it closes. This rule is called isochrony.' lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'The sound designer decides which sound plays for that name, in a program between the sound files and the game' presents middleware as always used. Many games use the game engine's own built-in audio tools instead, and the term list includes 'Built-in audio stack'. Flow 4: the music paragraph (5) says the game adds layers 'as the action becomes more intense' before paragraph 6 explains how the sound system learns what is happening, so the two paragraphs are in the wrong order. Paragraph 6 also ends on two add-on sentences (automatic mix changes and branching dialogue). Scope: the events and implementation, variation, spatial, interactive music, states and parameters, and budget groups are all present in proportion. Brands are correctly left to the flashcards. Glossary: all six named terms match their plain English, and occlusion is correctly kept separate from obstruction.
lessons.comment: A strong lesson. The organizing question, how sound can be ready for moments nobody can predict, carries the whole topic, and the language is literal and plain. Two small changes would make it ready for approval: add 'often' so middleware is not presented as universal, and put the states paragraph before the music paragraph. Overall: weighted 4.6, grade A.
lessons.fixes: ACCURACY: Change 'The sound designer decides which sound plays for that name, in a program between the sound files and the game.' to 'The sound designer decides which sound plays for that name, often in a program between the sound files and the game.' This adds 1 word and brings the lesson to 480, still within the limit. FLOW: Swap paragraphs 5 and 6. Change the opening of the moved states paragraph, 'The sound system also needs to know what is happening.', to 'To change sounds at the right moment, the sound system needs to know what is happening.' Change the opening of the moved music paragraph, 'Music must change too, because nobody knows when a fight will start.', to 'Music uses this information too, because nobody knows when a fight will start.' lessons.reasons: Scope 4: about 14 of the 105 terms (13%) are remote-control apps (MixPad, CQ-MixPad, SQ MixPad, Qu-Control, ProLink Console Remote, Remote control enable, OneMix, MyMon, CQ4You, Qu-You, SQ4You). lessons.comment: Accurate, well-ordered beginner lesson with a good everyday opening that ends on a clear question.
