lessons.reasons: Flow 4: paragraph 6 joins two separate ideas (frequency bands, then circuit design with 'The circuit design matters too'), and paragraph 7 puts transient shaping and artifacts together under one loose link, so both read as add-ons rather than answers to the previous paragraph. Clarity 4: the circuit list 'light, a transistor, a chip or vacuum tubes' names four parts a 16-year-old beginner does not know, and does not say what each part does (the part that turns the sound down).
lessons.comment: Weighted 4.7 (A). The check script passes: 479 words, 8 paragraphs, average sentence 14.1 words, 6 sentences over 20 words, no fails or warnings. All five named terms (threshold, compressor, limiter, gate, sidechain) exist in the 221-term list and agree with their plain English. Coverage of the large groups is in proportion: core controls, limiting and clipping, gates and expanders, detection and sidechain (including ducking and de-essing), multiband, circuit types, transients, and artifacts. Knee and feed-forward/feedback are not mentioned, but both groups are small and fit in the flashcards. Every claim is accurate. The lesson is at 479 words, so any fix must replace words, not add them.
lessons.fixes: Flow (paragraph 6): 'The circuit design matters too. Circuits that use light, a transistor, a chip or vacuum tubes each react at a typical speed.' -> 'Even with one band, the part inside that turns the sound down matters. It can use a light, a transistor, a chip or a vacuum tube, and each reacts at its own typical speed.' (this links it to the band idea before it and tells the beginner what the part does). Flow (paragraph 7): 'All these tools change how each sound rises and falls. Related tools raise or lower the start of each sound and the part after it, separately.' -> 'All these tools change how each sound rises and falls. A related tool, the transient shaper, raises or lowers the start of each sound and the part after it, separately.' (only if 'Transient Shaper' is wanted as a named term; it is in the list). Clarity: see the paragraph 6 fix above; it also covers the clarity point.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'The filter does not change what you hear.' Taken literally, this is misleading: a sidechain filter does change what you hear, because it changes how the compressor acts. Only the filtering itself is not applied to the audio. Also, 'to detect quick peaks better' undersells oversampling: the glossary says it catches peaks between samples and reduces the harsh distortion from clamping fast. Flow 4: the gate hysteresis sentences ('Timing also matters for a gate...') are a side step inside a compressor-timing paragraph, and the mid/side sentence at the end of paragraph 5 is added on with no link. Clarity 4: 'a higher sample rate inside' assumes the reader knows what a sample rate is, and 'Equipment compressors' is unclear (it means hardware units). Language 4: 'Equipment compressors' is not a natural phrase for a second-language reader, and 'The first step is how it decides.' is awkward when read literally.
lessons.comment: Weighted 4.4 (B). The check script passes: 479 words, 8 paragraphs, average sentence 12.9 words, 5 sentences over 20 words, no fails or warnings. The next-step opening is right for an advanced topic. All 94 terms' large groups are in the chain: sidechain filtering, timing and release, circuit character, split-band and mid/side, serial and clip-to-limit chains, and limiting (overshoot, look-ahead, oversampling). No brand names appear, even though the list includes the LA-2A, 1176 and Fairchild. All four named terms (sidechain, character, split-band compression, serial compression) agree with the glossary. The lesson is at 479 words, so fixes must replace words, not add them.
lessons.fixes: Accuracy: 'The filter does not change what you hear.' -> 'The filter changes only what the measuring part receives, not the sound itself.' Accuracy and clarity: 'Some also work at a higher sample rate inside, to detect quick peaks better.' -> 'Some also measure the sound in finer steps inside, to catch peaks that fall between the normal measuring points and to add less distortion.' Clarity and language: 'Equipment compressors usually turn the sound down with' -> 'Hardware compressors usually turn the sound down with'. Language: 'The first step is how it decides.' -> 'First, consider how it decides.' Flow: 'Timing also matters for a gate. It opens at one level but closes only at a lower level, so it does not switch on and off rapidly.' -> 'A gate uses a similar timing idea: it opens at one level but closes only at a lower level, so it does not switch on and off rapidly.' Flow: 'A stereo mix can also be divided into its center and its sides, each with its own compressor, and then joined again.' -> 'The same idea can divide a stereo mix by place instead of frequency: its center and its sides each get their own compressor, and then they are joined again.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Before recording, a separate head erases the old sound' reads literally as a separate step done before recording. The erase head actually works during recording, just ahead of the record head on the tape path. 'A small ring of magnetic metal' is also loose, since many heads are ferrite, a ceramic. Scope 4: all large groups are covered (transport, speed errors, heads and contact, azimuth and height, reference-tape calibration, bias). Two small groups are missing: zenith, which the Welcome names, and head magnetization and degaussing. Flow 4: paragraph 6 jumps from the reference tape to sync-head playback ('When new parts are added to a song...') with no link, so the sync-head sentence reads as a side item. Clarity 4: 'the tape stores sound unevenly' is vague about what bias fixes. Paragraph 7 packs erase, bias, bias calibration and the log into five short sentences. Language 4: 'whose spring is running down' is a phrasal verb with a non-literal meaning (rule 11). Glossary 5: capstan, wow, flutter, gap, azimuth alignment, crosstalk, sync-head alignment, bias calibration and reference tape all match their plain English. House rules 5: the check script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns, at 479 words and 8 paragraphs. That is at the word limit, so every fix must be word-neutral or shorter.
lessons.comment: A solid B (weighted 4.2). The chain from steady speed to heads, angle and calibration is clear and accurate overall, and the safety-free mechanical topic is pitched well for a beginner. Main polish: the erase-head timing, the abrupt sync-head sentence, and one phrasal verb in the opening. The bias explanation is close in wording to sibling 4450 ('steady tone too high for people to hear' compared with 'steady, very high tone that nobody can hear'). Keep 4440's version brief and calibration-focused so the two do not read as a repeat. Live check: 211 terms, matching the snapshot. Term names are from the base tables.
lessons.fixes: Accuracy: 'Before recording, a separate head erases the old sound.' -> 'Just before the record head, a separate head erases the old sound.' | Accuracy: 'A tape head is a small ring of magnetic metal with a very narrow opening' -> 'A tape head is a small ring of magnetic material with a very narrow opening' | Flow: 'When new parts are added to a song, the record head also plays the old tracks, so the parts stay in time.' -> 'The record head needs the same care, because when new parts are added to a song, it also plays the old tracks, so the parts stay in time.' (To stay at or under 480 words, cut 'The results are usually written in a log.' to 'The results are written in a log.' and remove 'Moving tape also wears the head down.') | Clarity: 'Without it, the tape stores sound unevenly, and that causes distortion.' -> 'Without it, quiet parts of the sound are stored less accurately than loud parts, and that causes distortion.' (balance the extra words with the cuts above) | Language: 'Imagine an old wind-up record player whose spring is running down.' -> 'Imagine an old wind-up record player whose spring is losing its power.' | Scope (optional, if words allow): add zenith to the height sentence: 'The head must also sit at the correct height and lean neither forward nor back.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Playback makes the opposite change' can be read as playback undoing the record boost exactly, which would leave the high-frequency loss uncorrected. The glossary says playback uses a matching standard curve, and record and playback together make the sound even. Scope 4: materials, magnetism, bias, noise and level, track formats and cassette types are covered. The equalization standards group (NAB, CCIR, IEC1, IEC2, DIN, AES, NARTB, and others), which the Welcome names, is reduced to 'the wrong playback setting', and the reader never learns that there are several standards. Tape thickness and playing length, and the older recording eras and formats, are not mentioned. Flow 4: 'Machines also need one shared normal level.' is a new idea inside the noise-and-saturation paragraph and does not follow from it. Clarity 4: remanence, coercivity and the bias process come in quick succession in paragraphs 3 and 4, which is dense for a beginner. Language 4: 'the tape lowers the loudest peaks' and 'Each format balances these limits in its own way' give the tape and the format agency (mild personification). Glossary 5: tape formulation, remanence, coercivity, biasing, record equalization, tape hiss, tape saturation, reference fluxivity, track configuration, base (Base film) and binder (Tape binder) all agree with the glossary. House rules 5: the script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns, at 478 words and 8 paragraphs. That is close to the limit.
lessons.comment: A solid B (weighted 4.2). The cassette opening is a fresh scene that differs from its siblings, and it leads to a clear question. The chain from materials to magnetism, bias, equalization, limits and formats is logical and accurate. Polish: make clear that playback uses a matching standard curve and that more than one standard exists. Also move the reference-level sentences so they do not interrupt the limits paragraph, and remove the two small personifications. Live check: 189 terms, matching the snapshot.
lessons.fixes: Accuracy and scope: 'So machines raise some frequencies while recording, which is called record equalization. Playback makes the opposite change. The wrong playback setting gives the wrong balance of low and high frequencies.' -> 'So machines raise some frequencies while recording, which is called record equalization. Playback uses a matching curve, so the final sound is even. There are several standard curves, and the wrong playback curve gives the wrong balance of low and high frequencies.' | Flow: 'Machines also need one shared normal level. A test tape holds a tone at one standard strength of magnetism, called reference fluxivity, and each machine is set to match it.' -> 'Between these limits, machines need one shared normal level. A test tape holds a tone at one standard strength of magnetism, called reference fluxivity, and each machine is set to match it.' (Or start a short paragraph with it; total stays at 8 paragraphs if merged.) | Language: 'the tape lowers the loudest peaks and adds extra tones' -> 'the loudest peaks are made lower and extra tones are added' | Language: 'Each format balances these limits in its own way.' -> 'Each format makes a different choice between these limits.' | Word budget: to stay at or under 480, shorten 'Imagine holding a cassette up to the light and seeing a thin brown tape between two small reels.' to 'Imagine holding a cassette up to the light and seeing the thin brown tape inside.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: binder decay, base decay, pack and winding defects, inspection, treatment and storage are all present, with the safety rule early. Damage to splices, leaders and edges is only listed in passing. Lubricant loss and mold are barely touched, although together they are a sizable share of the 169 terms. Flow 4: paragraph 5 is a two-sentence list ('checks the coating, the joins, the plain leader strips at each end, the reel and the case...') that reads as a side block. The last paragraph packs three ideas: storage conditions, print-through, and warming a cold tape. Clarity 4: 'storing the tape wound to its end makes the echo less noticeable' is unclear to a beginner. It does not say the end of the tape is on the outside of the reel, or why the echo becomes less noticeable (it falls after the sound instead of before it). Language 4: the same 'wound to its end' phrase is ambiguous when read literally. 'Tapes ... a high, loud noise' is fine. Opening and closing 4: the opening is strong. The closing introduces 'stabilized', a word the lesson never explained, and its summary leaves out inspection, which is a full paragraph. Accuracy 5: every claim checks out, including baking not being used on acetate, copying immediately after baking, upright reels, and slow warming in a sealed bag. Glossary 5: binder hydrolysis, sticky-shed syndrome, vinegar syndrome, tape pack, cinching, tape baking and print-through all match. House rules 5: the script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns, at exactly 480 words and 8 paragraphs. Any fix must be word-neutral or shorter.
lessons.comment: The strongest of the three (weighted 4.4, B, close to A). The opening is clear, the never-break rule ('stop the machine immediately') comes early inside the chain, and every claim is accurate. Polish: make the tail-out storage sentence literal, turn the inspection list into one linked sentence, and close with words the lesson has already used. The lesson is at the 480-word limit, so trim when adding. Live check: 169 terms, matching the snapshot.
lessons.fixes: Clarity and language: 'Cool storage helps limit it, and storing the tape wound to its end makes the echo less noticeable.' -> 'Cool storage helps limit it. Storing the tape with its end on the outside of the reel makes the echo come after each sound, where it is harder to hear.' | Flow: 'Because much of this damage is hidden, a tape is inspected before it is played. Someone checks the coating, the joins, the plain leader strips at each end, the reel and the case, and looks for mold or dirt.' -> 'Because much of this damage is hidden, a tape is inspected before it is played, from its coating, joins and end strips to its reel, case, mold and dirt.' (saves about 8 words for the fix above) | Opening and closing: 'By the end, you will know why a tape is checked and stabilized before it is played, and what keeps it safe for years.' -> 'By the end, you will know why a tape is inspected and treated before it is played, and what keeps it safe for years.' | Opening and closing: 'The flashcards explain each part in detail: decay and damage, cleaning and treatment, and storage.' -> 'The flashcards explain each part in detail: decay and damage, inspection, treatment, and storage.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the idea in the topic's own name, seismoacoustic coupling (one event making waves in both ground and air, each turning into the other: Air-to-ground coupling, Ground-to-air coupling, Seismoacoustic coupling/wavefield/data fusion, Ground-coupled acoustic wave), is never stated. Surface-process sources (landslide, rockfall, debris flow, avalanche, bedload, fluvial, sediment impact) are also absent; glaciers are the only one mentioned. Flow 4: paragraph 5 holds three ideas: long-range low sound, the microseism (a different signal from a different source), then sensor arrays. The microseism sentence breaks the line from 'low sounds travel far' to 'how to find the source'. Clarity 4: 'arrival times at known distances show what the rock is like' packs two steps into one clause, and a beginner cannot follow it on first read.
lessons.comment: Strong, accurate lesson with a good everyday opening and a clean exploration paragraph. All named terms match the glossary. It sits at 479 words, so any addition needs a matching cut. The fixes are about the ground-air link that names the topic, plus one crowded paragraph.
lessons.fixes: SCOPE: in paragraph 5, after 'Those low sounds can travel very far.' add: 'The same event often makes waves in both the ground and the air. Where the ground meets the air, one kind of wave can create the other.' In paragraph 3, after the glacier sentence, add: 'Landslides, rockfalls and rivers that roll stones also shake the ground.' To stay within 480 words, cut 'Inside a drilled hole, a tool times sound through the rock beside it. That record is called a sonic log.' down to 'A tool lowered into a drilled hole records a sonic log.' FLOW: move 'Ocean waves also make a faint, steady shaking of the ground, called a microseism.' to the end of paragraph 5 and reword it as 'Ocean waves also make a faint, steady shaking of the ground, called a microseism, which these sensors record all the time.' CLARITY: 'The speed of each wave depends on the rock, so arrival times at known distances show what the rock is like.' -> 'Each wave travels faster in some rocks than in others. So the time a wave takes to reach a sensor shows what kind of rock it passed through.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'Sound too weak to collapse bubbles can instead create a fixed pattern' suggests that the pattern comes from the sound being weak. In fact a standing pattern comes from sound reflecting back on itself; being gentle only keeps bubbles from collapsing. Also, 'a coating holds only the chosen molecules' is an absolute; real coatings are selective, not perfect. Scope 4: the light-and-sound group at the molecular scale (Phonon, Acoustic/Optical/Coherent phonon, Brillouin scattering/spectroscopy/microscopy, Hypersound, Picosecond ultrasonics, about 8% of the terms) is absent. It is under 10%, but it could be named in the closing. Flow 4: paragraph 4 moves from jets and cell disruption to standing-wave particle sorting halfway through, so two ideas share one paragraph. Clarity 4: 'How much sound energy the liquid absorbs shows how its molecules move.' is vague for a beginner.
lessons.comment: A clear chain from intense sound (bubbles, chemistry, jets) to gentle sound (measuring, sensing) to sound made by light. All named terms agree with the glossary. Two small accuracy wordings and one crowded paragraph remain.
lessons.fixes: ACCURACY: 'Sound too weak to collapse bubbles can instead create a fixed pattern of high and low pressure in the liquid.' -> 'Sound that reflects back on itself can create a fixed pattern of high and low pressure in the liquid. When this sound is too gentle to collapse bubbles,' (then continue: 'small particles collect at fixed places in that pattern.'). And 'where a coating holds only the chosen molecules' -> 'where a coating holds mainly the chosen molecules'. SCOPE: in the closing, change 'from bubbles and their chemistry to measuring and sensing with sound' -> 'from bubbles and their chemistry to measuring and sensing with sound, and even the tiny vibrations inside materials that scatter light'. FLOW: start the standing-wave material as its own short link at the start of paragraph 5 ('Gentler sound does not collapse bubbles. ...'), so paragraph 4 ends on 'mix liquids that normally stay separate.' CLARITY: 'How much sound energy the liquid absorbs shows how its molecules move.' -> 'The liquid also takes in a little of the sound energy. How much it takes in shows how its molecules move and react.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: covert devices and interception is the largest term group (bugs, transmitters, wiretaps, laser/spike/parabolic microphones, listening posts, about 25-30%), yet it gets one short paragraph. The legal-interception terms (Lawful interception, One-party consent, Consensual monitoring, Minimization, Title III intercept) are reduced to one vague sentence. Speaker comparison gets a similar amount of space with a smaller share of terms. Flow 4: 'Some recordings are made in secret.' pivots away from the courtroom recording that runs through paragraphs 1-5, so the covert half feels attached rather than grown from the thread. Clarity 4: paragraph 2 packs the original vs copy, re-save detection, background continuity and the electric network frequency into nine sentences. Language 4: 'a phone recording of an argument played in a court' can be read literally as an argument that was played in court.
lessons.comment: Accurate and careful lesson: the likelihood-ratio idea and the transcript-priming caution are well put, and all named terms match the glossary. The covert-capture half is thin for its share of the term list, and the opening sentence is ambiguous.
lessons.fixes: LANGUAGE: 'Imagine a phone recording of an argument played in a court.' -> 'Imagine a phone recording of an argument. It is played as evidence in a court.' FLOW: 'Some recordings are made in secret.' -> 'The recording in the court may itself have been made in secret.' SCOPE: replace 'Many countries have strict laws about this.' with 'Many countries allow secret recording only with a court order, or when at least one person in the conversation agrees.' Then add to paragraph 6: 'The sound may be stored, or sent to a listening post where someone hears it live.' CLARITY: split paragraph 2 after 'signs that the file was saved again in another format.' Start a new paragraph with 'In an untouched recording, the quiet background sound usually changes only slowly...' (still 8 paragraphs if the gunshot paragraph joins the speaker paragraph, or cut 'Examiners keep it unchanged and work on an exact copy.' to 'Examiners work only on an exact copy.' to keep the word count).

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the recording-session planning group (Session Plan, Recording Schedule, Pre-Production, Reference Track, Lyric Sheet, Input List, Demo) and the people and roles group (Stakeholder, RACI Matrix, Project Sponsor, crew calls) get almost no space, and quality methods (Six Sigma, Kaizen, DMAIC, PDCA Cycle) appear only in the closing. Flow 4: paragraph 5 (methods) is thin and could move without loss, and the link into paragraph 6 is forced. Language 4: 'meet problems' is a figure of speech, and 'the plan also sets travel' is not literal English. Opening/closing 4: the closing brings in 'methods for improving quality', which the body never covers. Accuracy, glossary and house rules are all clean: the six named terms match their plain English, the check script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns, and live count is 245.
lessons.comment: A clear, accurate chain (scope, estimate, order, method, logistics, risk, sign-off), and every named term matches the glossary. Weighted 4.5 (A). The live-event logistics paragraph fits the term list well. The weak spots are that recording-session planning is left out, the method paragraph is thin, and the closing names quality methods the body never mentions. The lesson is at 479 words, so any fix must be word-neutral or must cut words elsewhere.
lessons.fixes: Scope/Flow: 'To carry out this ordered plan, teams choose a method. Some finish each stage before the next one starts. Others work in short repeated rounds and check the result after each one.' -> 'To carry out this ordered plan, teams choose a method. Some finish each stage before the next one starts. Others work in short repeated rounds and check the result after each one. A recording project follows the same steps, with a session plan and a recording schedule.' (to pay for these words, cut 'Its shared documents, such as a stage map, also show which equipment to pack and which items to rent.' down to 'A stage map shows what equipment to bring.'). Language: 'Even a good plan can meet problems.' -> 'Even a good plan can have problems.' Language: 'So the plan also sets travel, hotel rooms and rest for the crew.' -> 'So the plan also includes travel, hotel rooms and rest for the crew.' Flow: 'This job is also in a venue in another city.' -> 'This job also takes place in a venue in another city.' (if the word budget allows, otherwise leave it). Opening/closing: 'from the first agreement and the people who approve it to methods for improving quality and the final approval' -> 'from the first agreement and the people who approve it to schedules, risks and the final approval'.

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the personal-attributes group (Adaptability, Resilience, Growth Mindset, Emotional Intelligence, Imposter Syndrome, Initiative, Critical Thinking) is about 10% of the 130 terms, but the chain does not cover it; it appears only as 'personal attitudes' in the closing. Flow 4: burnout is attached to the company-rules paragraph with 'You also need to protect your own health', which is a jump inside the paragraph, and 'Some of this work happens inside a company' links only loosely to mentorship. Opening/closing 4: the closing lists 'personal attitudes', which the body does not explain. Everything else is clean: the six named terms match their plain English (situational leadership and psychological safety are described without being named, and both are correct), the script passes, and live count is 130.
lessons.comment: Strong lesson: the two-engineers opening leads straight to the topic's question, and each paragraph grows from the last (habits, communication, team, reputation, learning, company). It is accurate and plain throughout. Weighted 4.6 (A). The small polish is to give personal attitudes a real place in the chain and to move burnout so it grows from that idea instead of being added to the company paragraph.
lessons.fixes: Scope/Flow: 'You also need to protect your own health. Long hours and stress over many months can make a person exhausted and no longer interested in the job. That condition is called burnout.' -> move this to the start of a short final body thread, before the closing: 'Behind all of these habits are personal attitudes, such as staying calm when plans change and believing you can keep learning. Those attitudes also need care. Long hours and stress over many months can make a person exhausted and no longer interested in the job. That condition is called burnout.' To stay at 480 words or fewer, shorten 'Conferences, workshops and professional organizations help you learn and meet other people who work in audio.' to 'Conferences and workshops help you learn and meet other people in audio.' Opening/closing: after the fix above, 'from daily habits, communication and personal attitudes to building a career and working inside a company' can stay as written.

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: 'Publishing' is in the title, but the lesson does not cover publishing agreements (Publishing Agreement, Co-publishing agreement, Publishing administration deal, Sub-publishing agreement); the contracts paragraph is almost all about the record label. Enforcement and exceptions (Fair Use, Public Domain, Copyright Infringement, DMCA takedown notice, Cease-and-desist letter) get only the words 'or a legal exception'. Accuracy is 5, with one note: 'A film needs permission for both the song and the recording' is true when a film uses an existing recording; it can stay because the paragraph is about a recorded song. Live count is 199, and the script passes with 0 fails and 0 warns.
lessons.comment: An excellent chain: ownership, permission, payment, collecting organizations, contracts. Each paragraph answers the question the previous one left, the two-copyrights idea is explained clearly, and recoupment matches its glossary meaning (no repayment from the artist's own pocket). Weighted 4.9 (A). The only polish is to give the publishing side of contracts one sentence, so the title's middle word is covered.
lessons.fixes: Scope: 'Co-writers usually write down each person's share.' -> 'Co-writers usually write down each person's share. A writer may also sign a publishing agreement, which gives a publisher part of the song's income for managing it.' To stay at 480 words or fewer (now 475), shorten 'A contract also sets how long the deal lasts and whether rights later return to the creator.' to 'A contract also sets how long the deal lasts.' Or cut 'In many countries, the recording also earns separate money for its owner and performers.' down to 'The recording also earns separate money for its owner and performers.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'After each stage, the owner sends a bill' is an absolute; many jobs are billed once at the end or at agreed milestones. Scope 4: the releases and distribution group (Electronic Press Kit, Pre-save campaign, Playlist pitching, Digital distribution aggregator, Impact date, Imprint) and the client-management group (Client Retention, Client intake form, Testimonial, Online Reviews) are packed into the last two sentences of the marketing paragraph. Flow 3: the quote paragraph runs backward ('A quote depends on a plan' comes after the quote is written), and the marketing paragraph jumps from a wedding keyboardist finding clients to releasing his own music on streaming services. A reader feels both jumps. Clarity 4: the marketing paragraph lists four channels, then own-music promotion, distribution and fans in a row. Language 4: 'Such an owner usually reaches streaming services' is vague and awkward. Glossary and house rules are clean: the named terms match their plain English, the script passes, and live count is 172.
lessons.comment: A sound business chain (legal form, prices, quote/invoice/deposit, profit and cash flow, taxes, marketing), and the named terms agree with the glossary. Weighted 4.1 (B). It needs a fix before approval: the quote-then-plan order is reversed, the invoicing statement is absolute, and the last body paragraph crowds marketing, own-music releases and recommendations together, with a jump the opening scene does not prepare for. The lesson is at 477 words, so the fixes below are written to be close to word-neutral.
lessons.fixes: Flow/Accuracy: 'A quote depends on a plan. The owner plans the dates, hires the musicians and lists each stage with its cost. After each stage, the owner sends a bill, called an invoice.' -> 'Once the client accepts the quote, the owner plans the dates, hires the musicians and lists each stage with its cost. After a stage or at the end, the owner sends a bill, called an invoice.' Flow/Clarity/Language: 'The same tools also promote the owner's own music. Such an owner usually reaches streaming services through a distribution company and tells fans before the release day. But much audio work comes from recommendations, so careful service keeps clients returning.' -> 'Many owners also release their own music. They usually send it to streaming services through a distribution company and tell fans before the release day. Still, much audio work comes from recommendations, so careful service keeps clients returning.' Clarity: 'A website, emails, social media and short news announcements for reporters help the right group of possible clients find the owner.' -> 'A website, emails and social media help the right clients find the owner.' (this cut also pays for the words added above).

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: it gives the wrong reason for the amplifier behind a condenser capsule. The glossary says the capsule signal is very weak AND very high-impedance, and the high impedance is the main reason a long cable cannot carry it. Scope 4: the MEMS group (about 30 of 180 terms) gets three short sentences. The other powering systems (T-power, A-B, plug-in power, battery) get one clause. Flow 4: the last chain paragraph joins two unrelated groups (piezo, then MEMS) with no link between them. Clarity 4: 'transformer' is used without a plain description. Language 4: the third sentence of the opening is confusing when read literally and changes tense. Opening/closing 4: that same broken sentence weakens an otherwise good opening.
lessons.comment: A strong, well-ordered chain from transducer to capsule, then dynamic/ribbon, condenser, electronics and powering, and finally other methods. Named terms match the glossary. The script passes (479 words, close to the limit). The main fixes are one confusing opening sentence, a fuller reason for the condenser amplifier, and a link sentence before MEMS.
lessons.fixes: 1) 'Your voice makes tiny, fast changes in air pressure. In between, moving air became an electrical signal.' -> 'Your voice makes tiny, fast changes in air pressure. Before the phone can store your voice, those changes must become an electrical signal.' 2) 'A condenser capsule's signal is very weak, so a long cable would lose much of it and add noise.' -> 'A condenser capsule's signal is very weak and cannot push current along a long cable, so the cable would lose much of it and add noise.' 3) 'Its signal is very small, so a transformer usually increases its voltage.' -> 'Its signal is very small, so a transformer, a part made of two coils of wire, usually increases its voltage.' 4) 'Most microphones in phones use the charge method at a very small size.' -> 'The charge method can also be made very small, and most microphones in phones use it.' (this links the MEMS sentences to the condenser paragraph; to stay under 480 words, cut 'It is hard to damage and needs no power.' to 'It needs no power.')

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the large testing/verification group (characterization, measurements, verification, environmental and stability testing, about 25 terms) gets only 'international standards describe each test' and one clause tacked onto the end of the mounts paragraph. Flow 4: paragraph 6 packs stand, boom, shockmount, windscreens, pop filter, rain/dust covers and heat/damp testing into one paragraph that reads like a list. The testing clause belongs with paragraph 4. Clarity 4: that same paragraph introduces too many objects at once. Language 4: 'one records much better' is a vague quality claim. Opening/closing 4: the opening promises that the sheet explains why one records 'much better', but the lesson never returns to that.
lessons.comment: Accurate and well matched to the glossary, with a clear first half (sensitivity, then self-noise, then dynamic range, then standards and matching). The second half has many items, and the testing group is underweighted. The script passes (478 words).
lessons.fixes: 1) 'They look almost the same, but one records much better.' -> 'They look almost the same, but one is quieter and handles loud sounds better.' 2) 'Other covers protect it from rain and dust, and makers test how heat and damp air change its performance.' -> 'Other covers protect it from rain and dust.' Then move the testing idea into paragraph 4: after 'So international standards describe each test.' add 'Makers also test how heat, damp air and shocks change these numbers over time.' 3) In paragraph 6, to reduce density, cut 'A stand, often with a long arm called a boom, holds the microphone in position. But the vibration' -> 'A stand holds the microphone in position, but the vibration'. This keeps the paragraph on one thread: noise from the stand, then from air.

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: it says main microphones record little of the room. Main arrays (for example a spaced tree above an orchestra) usually record a large part of the hall sound. Scope 4: ambience, room and surround/height arrays (about 45 of 263 terms) get three short sentences at the end, less than their share. Flow 4: paragraph 5 packs spot microphone, bleed, the closer-than rule and frequency cancellation into one paragraph. Clarity 4: 'Adding and subtracting their signals makes left and right' is hard for a beginner to picture without one more plain clause. Language 4: 'the center sounding empty' and 'pulled toward' are slightly figurative.
lessons.comment: An excellent opening (eyes closed in a hall, then two ear clues) that organizes the whole stereo section well. Precedence and spot delay are explained correctly. It is a little crowded in the middle and light on room and surround arrays. The script passes (8 paragraphs, 476 words).
lessons.fixes: 1) 'Close and main microphones record little of the room itself, so microphones farther back record its reflections and applause.' -> 'Close microphones record little of the room, and main microphones record only part of it, so microphones farther back record more of its reflections and applause.' 2) 'A very large gap can leave the center sounding empty, with instruments pulled toward the left or right.' -> 'A very large gap can make few sounds seem to come from the center, and instruments seem to come only from the left or right.' 3) 'Adding and subtracting their signals makes left and right.' -> 'Adding the two signals gives the left channel, and subtracting them gives the right channel.' 4) Paragraph 5: move 'When the same sound reaches two microphones at different times, mixing them cancels some frequencies.' to the start of paragraph 6, just before 'Timing matters in a second way.' Or, to save words, cut it and change 'Timing matters in a second way.' to 'Timing also matters.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'its sound comes from one speaker' is an absolute that is often false (many guitar cabinets hold two or four speakers, and one of them is chosen for miking). 'The same ideas often guide miking a ukulele or a banjo' is weak for the banjo, which has a head and no sound hole. Scope 4: pickup-microphone blends (three terms), reamping (two) and isolation cabinets (two) are missing. Harp and oud are not hinted at. Flow 4: 'Engineers use the word miking for placing microphones' interrupts the opening scene. Clarity 4: the opening paragraph packs scene, definition and question together. Language 4: 'the low frequencies cover the rest of the sound' is figurative.
lessons.comment: A clear, accurate-in-the-main tour from the speaker cone to acoustic guitar, bowed strings and internal microphones. The common-starting-point framing is correct, and all five named terms match the glossary. Small fixes cover one absolute, one figurative verb and a few small missing groups. The script passes (478 words).
lessons.fixes: 1) 'because its sound comes from one speaker in the amplifier's cabinet.' -> 'because the microphone is usually aimed at one speaker in the amplifier's cabinet.' 2) 'so the low frequencies cover the rest of the sound.' -> 'so the low frequencies are so loud that the rest of the sound is hard to hear.' 3) 'The same ideas often guide miking a ukulele or a banjo.' -> 'The same ideas often guide miking a ukulele and other small guitars.' 4) 'Engineers use the word miking for placing microphones. A microphone very close' -> 'Placing microphones is called miking. A microphone very close' (or fold the definition into the question at the end of the paragraph). 5) Internal-microphone paragraph: 'so it is often mixed with a microphone outside the instrument.' -> 'so it is often mixed with a microphone outside the instrument, or with a pickup that senses the strings.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the recording-workflow group (tracking, overdub, double tracking, print, record safe, multitrack, about 15% of the 101 live terms) gets only a side clause in the cue-mix paragraph and is never framed as its own link, although the Welcome text names tracking, overdubbing and printing. Flow 4: paragraph 3 jumps ahead to mixing (stems, hardware summing, hybrid mixing) in the middle of the recording path, then paragraph 4 goes back with 'Next, converters'; the remote-producer sentence at the end of paragraph 7 is tacked on. Clarity 4: paragraph 3 puts stems, adding tracks together in hardware and hybrid mixing into three short sentences, which is too much for a beginner. Language 4: 'So many interfaces' can be read as 'very many interfaces'; 'the hiss' appears with no introduction; 'A large group is stable' reads literally as the group being stable. Glossary 4: the DI box is described as changing the signal 'so the preamp can accept it', but the glossary's plain English for Direct injection is about letting the signal travel far with less hum. Opening/closing 4: the closing is generic ('each stage of this chain') and does not say in plain words that the flashcards also cover headphone mixes, monitoring and recording workflows. House rules 5: the script passes with 0 fails and 0 warnings. Note that 480 words and 8 paragraphs are both at the upper limit (the brief aims for 420-460 words and 7 paragraphs), so any fix should keep the word count the same or lower it.
lessons.comment: A strong, accurate lesson with a clear everyday opening (a phone voice message) and a real signal-path chain from preamp to converters, buffer, cue mix and control room. Every named term exists in the live list (101 terms, which matches the snapshot) and matches its glossary meaning. The main weakness is paragraph 3, which jumps ahead to mixing and then returns to recording. Recording workflows (tracking, overdubbing, printing) need a slightly clearer place in the chain. A few literal-reading problems remain. Weighted score 4.3 (B).
lessons.fixes:
Flow/Clarity (para 3): "During mixing, groups of tracks called stems may pass through hardware again. They may also be added together in hardware instead of in the computer. Mixing partly in hardware like this is called hybrid mixing." -> "Later, during mixing, some tracks may go out through this hardware again while the rest stay in the computer. Mixing partly in hardware like this is called hybrid mixing." (This removes the stems and summing detail, which the flashcards teach, and saves about 15 words.)
Scope (para 3, after 'so engineers often use only a little.'): add "Saving a sound with its processing already in it is called printing." (Term 'Print'; use the words saved in the fix above.)
Scope (para 6): "It matters most when new parts are recorded over earlier ones, or when the singer records the same part again on a second track." -> "It matters most during overdubbing, when new parts are recorded while the singer listens to earlier ones, or when the same part is sung again on a second track."
Language (para 5): "So many interfaces send the microphone straight to the headphones, skipping the computer." -> "For this reason, many interfaces send the microphone signal straight to the headphones, without passing through the computer."
Language (para 2): "Too little level leaves the signal close to the hiss." -> "Too little level leaves the signal close to the background noise."
Language (para 5): "A large group is stable but adds delay." -> "A large group lets the computer work without errors, but it adds delay."
Glossary (para 2): "through a small box that changes its signal so the preamp can accept it." -> "through a small box that changes its signal so it can travel through long cables with less hum."
Flow (para 7): "These headphone and speaker feeds can also be sent over the internet to a producer in another place." -> "The same listening feed can also be sent over the internet, so a producer in another place hears what the engineer hears."
Closing (para 8): "The flashcards explain each stage of this chain in detail." -> "The flashcards explain each stage of this chain, the headphone and speaker feeds, and the common ways a song is recorded part by part."

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: the dynamic EQ description is narrower than the truth and than the glossary. A dynamic band can also act when a range gets too quiet, and it can boost as well as cut. 'Shift some frequencies slightly later' is an acceptable simplification of phase shift. Scope 4: the live total of 333 terms matches the snapshot. Band shapes, controls, EQ types, phase and filter designs are covered well. Two large groups get little or no space. The adaptive and spectral group (match EQ, spectral matching, resonance suppression, tilt EQ, about 25 terms) gets one sentence through dynamic EQ. Mid/side EQ and analyzer views (RTA, 1/3-octave) are missing; only one closing sentence on room measurement touches the analyzer side. Flow 4: paragraph 5 lists three filter designs without names, so it reads as a side list. Paragraph 6 is a two-sentence add-on that could move without loss. Clarity 4: paragraph 2 names five shapes in one paragraph (bell, low shelf, high shelf, filter, notch). The lesson has 9 named terms, which is dense for a beginner. Language 4: 'gives up something to gain something else' is a phrasal verb with a non-literal meaning. 'Sharp drum hit' uses 'sharp' as a loose sound word. Glossary 4: dynamic equalization disagrees in part with its plain English ('only acts when a band gets too loud or too quiet'). House rules 4: the check script passes, but 480 words is at the very top of the range, and 9 named terms is above the standard's 2–6.
lessons.comment: Grade B (weighted 4.1). A clear, accurate and broad introduction to EQ with a good everyday opening and a correct closing. The weak points are a packed shapes paragraph, an unnamed list of filter designs, a two-sentence dynamic-EQ add-on that is narrower than the glossary, and too many named terms at the word limit. The adaptive/spectral and mid/side corners of the topic are under-represented.
lessons.fixes: (1) Accuracy/Glossary: 'One band can lower its own frequencies only when they get too loud. That is called dynamic equalization.' -> 'A band can also change its level only when its frequencies become too loud or too quiet. That is called dynamic equalization.' (2) Flow/Scope: merge paragraph 6 into paragraph 7 and give it the adaptive group, e.g. 'Some problems appear only sometimes, such as one loud note. A band can change its level only when its frequencies become too loud or too quiet. That is called dynamic equalization. Other tools compare a sound with a target and adjust many bands at once.' This brings the lesson back to 7 paragraphs. (3) Language: 'Each filter design gives up something to gain something else.' -> 'Each filter design has an advantage and a cost.' (4) Language: 'a faint sound just before a sharp drum hit' -> 'a faint sound just before a sudden drum hit'. (5) Clarity/House rules (named-term count): 'Another shape raises or lowers everything below a chosen frequency, and it is called a low shelf. The same change above a chosen frequency is called a high shelf.' -> 'Another shape, called a shelf, raises or lowers everything below or above a chosen frequency.' Also, in paragraph 4, describe linear phase without the 'called' naming. Together these bring the named terms to about 7 and save words. (6) Scope (mid/side): in paragraph 7, after the masking sentence, add 'An equalizer can also treat the center of a stereo mix differently from its sides.' Pay for it by cutting 'Other changes are creative, such as more high frequencies on a voice.' to 'Other changes are creative.'

lessons.reasons: Scope 4: the live total of 113 terms matches the snapshot. Every large group is present: saturation/distortion, modulation, pitch/formant/vocoder, spectral, edits/reverse and transitions. But saturation/distortion is the largest group (drive, fuzz, clipping, waveshaping, exciters, tape, bitcrusher, about 28% of the terms) and gets only about 15% of the text. Ring modulation, frequency shifting and the talk box are missing. Flow 4: paragraphs 2–6 read as a catalogue of effect families. Paragraph 4 starts 'Pitch shifting can move…' with no link to the phaser sentence before it, and paragraphs 3 and 5 could be swapped without loss. Clarity 4: the phaser sentence ('a copy that is shifted in time by a different amount at each frequency') is dense for a beginner. Language 4: 'strong distortion' uses 'strong', a vague sound adjective listed in rule 12.
lessons.comment: Grade B (weighted 4.4). An accurate lesson in plain English that covers the whole topic. Named terms agree with the glossary, and the opening and closing are good. The main weaknesses are a list-like middle with weak links between paragraphs, an under-weighted saturation/distortion group, one vague adjective, and one dense phaser sentence.
lessons.fixes: (1) Language: 'Much more of it creates strong distortion.' -> 'Much more of it creates heavy distortion, which changes the sound a lot.' (better: 'Much more of it creates distortion, which changes the wave shape a lot.'). (2) Flow: 'Pitch shifting can move the whole sound higher or lower without changing its length.' -> 'Other effects change the pitch itself, not only slightly. Pitch shifting can move the whole sound higher or lower without changing its length.' (3) Flow: 'Some digital tools split a sound into many narrow frequency bands and change each band.' -> 'A vocoder works with frequency bands, and some digital tools go further. They split a sound into many narrow frequency bands and change each band.' (4) Clarity: 'A phaser mixes the sound with a copy that is shifted in time by a different amount at each frequency.' -> 'A phaser mixes the sound with a copy of itself. The copy is delayed by a different small amount at each frequency.' (5) Scope (saturation weight): after 'Other tools lower the sound quality on purpose.' add 'Some tools add these new frequencies only in one frequency range, so only part of the sound changes.' To stay at or under 480 words, cut 'Here the effects are part of the music itself.' from paragraph 1. (6) Scope (optional): in paragraph 3, after the tremolo sentence, add 'Another effect multiplies the sound by a steady tone, which creates new frequencies that are not musical notes.' (ring modulator). Pay for it by shortening the rotating-speaker sentence to 'A rotating speaker moves all three together.'

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: paragraph 5 says low-rate encoders send descriptions 'instead of full sound', but parametric stereo and bandwidth extension replace only parts of the signal (the stereo image, the high band). The core audio is still coded. Scope 4: the bitstream and syntax group (access unit, audio frame, sync word, elementary stream, profile-level indication, preroll, channel element and others, about 18% of 109 terms) and the quality-evaluation group (MOS, PEAQ, PESQ, POLQA, ODG) are squeezed into the last body paragraph. Multichannel and joint-stereo coding (intensity stereo, interchannel cues, coupled channels, downmixes) appears only through parametric stereo. Flow 4: paragraph 7 is a catch-all that holds five separate ideas (standards, frames, header, lossless coding, evaluation), so the lossless and evaluation sentences read as side items. Clarity 4: the CELP sentence ('a filter that copies the shape of the throat and mouth, with a chosen signal sent into it') is hard for a beginner, and the term is named without the reader seeing why it is called 'code-excited'.
lessons.comment: Strong, accurate chain from masking to filter bank, scalefactor, pre-echo, parametric tools and then speech coding. Every named term matches the glossary, and the script shows 0 fails and 0 warns at 476 words in 8 paragraphs. Term count checked live: 109. The main weakness is the crowded last body paragraph, which underplays the large bitstream/frame group and the quality-evaluation group.
lessons.fixes: Accuracy: "At low data rates, encoders send short descriptions instead of full sound." -> "At low data rates, encoders code only part of the sound fully and send short descriptions for the rest." | Scope/Flow: split paragraph 7 into two linked paragraphs. (a) "Each standard combines some of these methods for one job, such as streaming or phone calls, and describes how the coded data must be read. The coded data is usually organized in small blocks, each called an audio frame. Each frame starts with a fixed pattern that helps the decoder find it, and a setup header tells the decoder the coding type, sample rate and channels." (b) "Some standards also offer lossless coding, which makes the data smaller without changing the sound at all. For all the other methods, people need to know how much the sound has changed. Listeners score coded sound against the original, and computer models of hearing estimate the same score." Keep the total under 480 words by trimming paragraph 4's last sentence to "Shorter blocks reduce it." | Scope: in paragraph 5, after the parametric stereo sentence, add a short clause for joint stereo: "At higher data rates, encoders can still save data by coding what the two channels share only once." | Clarity: "Speech codecs model the voice as a filter that copies the shape of the throat and mouth, with a chosen signal sent into it." -> "Speech codecs treat the voice as two parts: a sound source, and a filter that shapes it the way the throat and mouth do. The encoder chooses the source signal from a stored list of codes."

lessons.reasons: Accuracy 4: 'so that no single group can control the result' is an absolute, because open processes aim at balance and do not guarantee it. Also, 'a ratio ... says how many times larger a value is' followed by the bel lets a reader think 2 bels means twice the power, since the counting-by-tens step is not stated. lessons.fixes: 'Single instruments may get small tone changes and a place from left to right, so they sound clear but still natural.' -> 'Single instruments, in an orchestra or in a small acoustic group, may get small tone changes and a place from left to right. A close microphone can also be mixed with a cable signal from the instrument, so it sounds clear but still natural.' | 'so some frequencies partly cancel and the sound becomes thinner' -> 'so some frequencies partly cancel and the sound loses some of its low and middle frequencies' | 'Strong "s" sounds are often reduced' -> 'Loud "s" sounds are often reduced' | 'The flashcards cover each step in detail, and separate files for each section.' -> 'The flashcards cover each step in detail, for orchestras, choirs and smaller acoustic groups.' (trim elsewhere to stay at 480 or fewer)

lessons.reasons: Flow 4: paragraph 3 ends with a list of editing actions plus a separate idea, 'You can also compare a new version with the old one.'. Clarity 4: 'Another setting starts recording...' makes latch sound like a separate setting, when it is one more choice of the same per-track mode setting. Also, 'decides what happens when you touch a control' does not fit the play-back-only choice. Opening/closing 4: the closing adds a vague new idea, 'the extra versions made at the end', without explaining it.
lessons.comment: Covers the whole topic in proportion: automation modes and passes, editing, mix bus and headroom, limiting and streaming loudness, translation and reference. Accurate, including the care taken with 'output or file' for clipping. Named terms match the glossary. Small wording fixes only. Script: 480 words (at the limit), 7 paragraphs, 0 fails.
lessons.fixes: 'A setting on each track decides what happens when you touch a control. It can play back only, replace every move, or record only while your hand is on the control. Another setting starts recording when you touch a control.' -> 'A setting on each track, called its mode, decides what the track does with recorded moves. It can play back only, replace every move, or record only while your hand is on the control. One more choice starts recording when you touch a control.' | 'You can drag these points, draw a slow rise, or copy moves to another chorus. You can also compare a new version with the old one.' -> 'You can drag these points, draw a slow rise, or copy moves to another chorus.' | 'The flashcards explain each step in detail, and the extra versions made at the end.' -> 'The flashcards explain each step in detail, and the extra versions of a mix, such as one with the voice louder.' (keep the total at 480 or fewer)

lessons.reasons: Clarity 4: 'the lathe receives the music slightly early' will confuse a beginner. It does not say how, or that the machine looks ahead at the music before it cuts. Opening/closing 4: the opening assumes the reader already knows what a 'master' is, and it starts from a statement, not from something the reader already knows. Batch 7 topics are not next-step topics, so the rule asks for an everyday starting point.
lessons.comment: Accurate and in proportion: lathe and lacquer, groove spacing and its limits, bass and 's' control, plating and test pressings, then the compact disc master, glass master and error checks. Named terms agree with the glossary (groove pitch, inner groove distortion, elliptical filter). Only the look-ahead sentence and the opening need plain-English work. Script: 470 words, 8 paragraphs, 0 fails.
lessons.fixes: 'So the lathe receives the music slightly early and spreads the turns apart before loud parts.' -> 'So the lathe gets a copy of the music a moment before it cuts it. That way it can spread the turns apart before a loud part arrives.' | 'A master for streaming is a computer file. A vinyl record or a compact disc is a physical object, so a physical master must be made first and then copied in a factory.' -> 'Imagine holding a vinyl record and a compact disc. The finished song, called the master, is first a computer file. A record or a disc is a physical object, so a physical version of the master must be made first and then copied in a factory.'
